"Rujjat al-ardu" means the earth was shaken and set in violent motion, to the point that buildings collapse and mountains fall down. "Bussat al-jibal" means they were crumbled to pieces; it was also said they were set moving, from the saying "bassa al-ghanam," meaning he drove the sheep. It is also said that "rujjat al-ardu" and "bussat al-jibal" are intransitive.

"Al-mash'amah" derives from "al-shu'm" (ill omen), or from "the left hand" (al-yad al-shu'ma), which is the left side.

"Al-thullalah" means a group, whether large or small. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Al-ummah" among people is a great multitude. The poet said:

Three Khandaqiyyah came to them, with an army like a flood torrent, foaming.

"Al-mawdunah" means woven with the parts of it fitted one upon another, like the links of a coat of mail. Al-A'sha said:

And of the weaving of Dawud, a mawdunah, moving with the tribe, camel after camel.

From this comes "wadin al-naqah," which is the girth of the she-camel, because it is mawdun, meaning twisted. The reciter said:

Toward you she goes, restless, her girth, with her unborn young lying across her belly.

Her religion opposes the religion of the Christians.

"Al-ibriq" is on the pattern "if'il" from "al-bariq" (gleam); it is a vessel for drinking with a spout. It was said it also has a handle. It is one of the wine vessels among the Arabs. The poet said:

As if their ewer were a gazelle upon a height, its neck bent, daubed with the cloth of cotton, its mouth crushed.

Adi ibn Zayd said:

We call to the morning, and there came a slave-girl with a ewer in her right hand.

"Suddi'a al-qawm bil-khamr" means the people were struck with headache from it. It was also said: "suddi'u" means they were scattered.

"Al-sidr" was discussed earlier in Surat Saba'.

"Al-makhdud" means the one whose thorns have been cut off. Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:

Indeed the gardens in the Paradises are shaded, in them are maidens whose lote-trees are without thorns.

"Al-talh" is the banana tree; it was also said it is a tree of the acacia kind with many thorns.

"Al-maskub" means poured out.

"Al-'arub" means one who is loving toward her husband.

"Al-tirb" means delight. It also refers to one who is born at the same time as another, and both were named so because they touched the dust at the same time. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

This surah is Meccan, and its connection to what precedes it is that it includes the punishment of the criminals and the bliss of the believers. He distinguished between the two gardens of some believers and the two gardens of others by His saying: ﴿And besides these two, there are two other gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 62]. Thus the world is divided into disbelievers, lesser believers, and superior believers. Likewise, the opening of this surah describes them as companions of the right hand, companions of the left hand, and the foremost, who are the ones brought near, and the companions of the right hand; and it ends with the deniers.

Ibn Abbas said: "Al-Waqi'ah" is one of the names of the Resurrection, like "al-Sakhkhah," "al-Tammah," and "al-Azifah," and these names indicate the greatness of its matter. The meaning of ﴿When the Event occurs﴾ is: when the one that must occur occurs, as you say: "The event happened," and "what was to be, was." The occurrence of a matter is its descent; it is said: "What I was expecting has occurred," meaning what I was awaiting has come down.

Al-Dahhak said: "Al-Waqi'ah" is the Cry, which is the blast in the Trumpet. It was also said: "Al-Waqi'ah" is the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis, which will fall on the Day of Resurrection.

The governing element of "idha" is the verb after it, as we have established in the books of grammar. It is in a position of genitive by the attachment of "idha" to it, so it needs a supposed governing element, since it is apparent that there is no spoken apodosis that governs it. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "By what is idha in the accusative?" I say: "By laysa (is not), like your saying: 'On Friday, I have no business,' or by an elided element, meaning: when it occurs, such and such will happen; or by implying 'udhkur' (mention)." End of quote.

As for its being in the accusative by "laysa," no grammarian, nor anyone who has a share of the discipline of i'rab (grammatical inflection), goes to such a view, because "laysa" in negation, like "kama" and "ma," does not govern. Likewise "laysa," because "laysa" is stripped of indicating an event and a time. The claim that it is a verb is metaphorical, because the definition of a verb does not apply to it. The governing element of an adverbial of time is only the event that takes place in it: when you say, "I will stand on Friday," standing takes place on Friday, and there is no event in "laysa," so how can it govern the adverbial? The example he compared it to, namely "On the Day of Resurrection, I have no business," does not indicate that "Friday" is accusative by "laysa." Rather, it is accusative by the governing element of the predicate of "laysa," which is the prepositional phrase, so it is a case of fronting the complement of the predicate before "laysa." The fronting of such is based on the permissibility of fronting the predicate of "laysa" before it, which is disputed, and it was not heard from the speech of the Arabs: "Standing, Zayd is not." "Laysa" indicates only the negation of the predicate's judgment about the subject, like "kama," but when pronoun endings attach to it, some people made it a verb, while in reality it is a particle of negation like "ma" (not).

It appears from al-Zamakhshari's illustration of "idha" with his saying "On Friday" that he deprived it of indicating the condition, which is its predominant meaning. Had it been a conditional, and the apodosis been the sentence introduced by "laysa," the particle "fa" would have been required, unless it is elided in poetry, as that occurs. So we say: "When Zayd treats you well, you will not leave his reward," and it is not permissible to say "lasta" without "fa" except in cases of necessity. As for his assumption, "When it occurs, such and such will happen," it indicates that in his view "idha" is conditional, and for that reason he supposed for it an apodosis that governs it. As for his saying "by implying udhkur," it strips it of being an adverbial and makes it a direct object in the accusative governed by "udhkur."

"Kadhibah": its apparent sense is that it is an active participle from "kadhaba," and it is an adjective of an elided noun. Al-Zamakhshari supposed it to be "nafs kadhibah" (a lying soul), meaning that when it occurs there will be no soul that lies about Allah, or lies in denying the unseen, because at that time every soul will be believing and truthful, whereas most souls today are liars and deniers, according to His saying: ﴿So when they saw Our might, they said: "We believe in Allah alone"﴾ [Ghafir: 84]; ﴿They will not believe in it until they see the painful punishment﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 201]; ﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease to be in doubt about it until the Hour comes upon them﴾ [al-Hajj: 55]. The "lam" is like it in His saying: ﴿Oh, I wish I had sent forth for my life﴾ [al-Fajr: 24], since there will be no soul for it that lies to it and says to it: "You did not lie," as today there are many souls that say to it: "You did not lie." Or it is from their saying: "His soul deceived him in a great matter," when it encourages him to undertake it and says to him: "You can bear it and what is beyond it," so he approaches it without care, in the sense that it is an event that cannot be endured because of its severity and horror, and that no soul at that time will encourage its owner with what it says to him in great matters, and make him think he can bear and endure it, because on that day they will be weaker and more humbled than that. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Like scattered moths﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 4]? Moths are a symbol of weakness. End of quote. It is excessive and verbose.

Ibn Atiyyah supposed it as a circumstantial "hal kadhibah" (a lying state), and said: The statement may have two meanings in this case. One is "kadhibah," meaning something lied about in what is reported concerning it, so it is called a lie for this reason, as you say: "This is a lying story," meaning it is a story in which there is lying. The second is "hal kadhibah," meaning its occurrence will not be delayed, as you say: "Such a one, when he takes on a task, does not fail." Qatadah and al-Hasan said: The meaning is: there is no denial of it, no refusal, and no postponement, so "kadhibah" in this case is a verbal noun, like "al-'aqibah," "al-'afiyah," and "khaizanat al-a'yun" (the treachery of the eyes). The sentence ﴿There will be no denying its occurrence﴾, according to what al-Zamakhshari supposed, that "idha" is governed by "laysa," would be the beginning of the surah, unless it is believed to be the apodosis of "idha," or governed by "udhkur," in which case it would not be the beginning of a speech. Ibn Atiyyah said: It is in the position of a circumstantial clause. What appears to me is that it is a parenthetical sentence between the conditional and its apodosis.

The majority read ﴿khāfiḍatun rāfiʿatun﴾ with both words in the nominative (rafʿ), taking them as predicates of an implied subject, "it is" (hiya). Zayd ibn ʿAlī, al-Ḥasan, ʿĪsā, Abū Ḥaywa, Ibn Abī ʿAbla, Ibn Miqsam, al-Zaʿfarānī, and al-Yazīdī in his own choice of reading, read them with the accusative (naṣb). Ibn Khālawayh said: al-Kisāʾī said, "Had al-Yazīdī not preceded me to it, I would have read it that way." The accusative here is in the position of the circumstantial accusative (ḥāl, a word describing the state of the subject at the time of the action).

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "This comes after the ḥāl that is ﴿laysa li-waqʿatihā kādhibatun﴾ ('no denying its occurrence'). You may also continue the ḥālāt (circumstantial clauses), just as you may continue the predicates (akhbār) of a subject. The first reading is more famous and more striking in meaning, because the position of the ḥāl in speech is the position of something which, if left unmentioned, would be dispensed with, while the position of the clauses that state a fact with certainty is the position of something of concern." End of quotation.

This point that he made was preceded by Abū al-Faḍl al-Rāzī. In Kitāb al-Lawāmiḥ he said: "The one who is in the ḥāl is the event (al-wāqiʿa), and the agent is 'waqaʿat' (it occurred). It is also permissible that ﴿laysa li-waqʿatihā kādhibatun﴾ be another ḥāl of al-wāqiʿa, with the implied sense: 'when the event occurs, truthfully.' These are three ḥālāt of one subject. It is permissible for different ḥālāt to come from one subject, just as different adjectives (nuʿūt) that are opposite to each other, and many predicates (akhbār), may come from one subject. When all of these are taken as ḥālāt, the governing agent of ﴿idhā waqaʿat﴾ ('when it occurs') is omitted, indicated by the context, with the implied sense of 'they will be called to account' or something similar." End of quotation.

The enumeration of the ḥālāt and predicates in this respect is disputed and detailed, and it is discussed in grammar (naḥw). Therefore this is not something on which the grammarians are agreed.

The majority said: On the Day of Resurrection, the heaven, the earth, and the mountains will be torn apart (tanfaṭiru) by it, and this structure will be broken down (tanhaddu) by it, through the raising of some bodies and the lowering of others. It is thus an expression of the intensity of the terror and turmoil.

Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: The Blast (al-ṣayḥa) lowers its force so that those nearest hear it, and raises it so that those farthest hear it.

Qatāda and ʿUthmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Surāqa said: The Resurrection lowers some peoples to the Fire and raises other peoples to the Garden.

Al-Zamakhsharī took these statements, as is his habit, and clothed them in some striking wording. He said: "It raises some peoples and lowers others. Either this describes it as severe, because great events are like that: some people rise to high ranks in them and others are brought low; or the wretched are brought down to the lowest depths (al-darakāt) and the blessed are raised to the degrees (al-darajāt). Or it is that it shakes things from their places, so that it lowers some and raises others, since it casts down the heaven in pieces (kisafan), scatters the stars and causes them to fall, and sets the mountains moving so that they pass through the air like clouds." End of quotation.

This surah is Meccan, and its connection to what precedes it is that it includes the punishment of the criminals and the bliss of the believers. He distinguished between the two gardens of some believers and the two gardens of others by His saying: ﴿And besides these two, there are two other gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 62]. Thus the world is divided into disbelievers, lesser believers, and superior believers. Likewise, the opening of this surah describes them as companions of the right hand, companions of the left hand, and the foremost, who are the ones brought near, and the companions of the right hand; and it ends with the deniers.

Ibn Abbas said: "Al-Waqi'ah" is one of the names of the Resurrection, like "al-Sakhkhah," "al-Tammah," and "al-Azifah," and these names indicate the greatness of its matter. The meaning of ﴿When the Event occurs﴾ is: when the one that must occur occurs, as you say: "The event happened," and "what was to be, was." The occurrence of a matter is its descent; it is said: "What I was expecting has occurred," meaning what I was awaiting has come down.

Al-Dahhak said: "Al-Waqi'ah" is the Cry, which is the blast in the Trumpet. It was also said: "Al-Waqi'ah" is the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis, which will fall on the Day of Resurrection.

The governing element of "idha" is the verb after it, as we have established in the books of grammar. It is in a position of genitive by the attachment of "idha" to it, so it needs a supposed governing element, since it is apparent that there is no spoken apodosis that governs it. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "By what is idha in the accusative?" I say: "By laysa (is not), like your saying: 'On Friday, I have no business,' or by an elided element, meaning: when it occurs, such and such will happen; or by implying 'udhkur' (mention)." End of quote.

As for its being in the accusative by "laysa," no grammarian, nor anyone who has a share of the discipline of i'rab (grammatical inflection), goes to such a view, because "laysa" in negation, like "kama" and "ma," does not govern. Likewise "laysa," because "laysa" is stripped of indicating an event and a time. The claim that it is a verb is metaphorical, because the definition of a verb does not apply to it. The governing element of an adverbial of time is only the event that takes place in it: when you say, "I will stand on Friday," standing takes place on Friday, and there is no event in "laysa," so how can it govern the adverbial? The example he compared it to, namely "On the Day of Resurrection, I have no business," does not indicate that "Friday" is accusative by "laysa." Rather, it is accusative by the governing element of the predicate of "laysa," which is the prepositional phrase, so it is a case of fronting the complement of the predicate before "laysa." The fronting of such is based on the permissibility of fronting the predicate of "laysa" before it, which is disputed, and it was not heard from the speech of the Arabs: "Standing, Zayd is not." "Laysa" indicates only the negation of the predicate's judgment about the subject, like "kama," but when pronoun endings attach to it, some people made it a verb, while in reality it is a particle of negation like "ma" (not).

It appears from al-Zamakhshari's illustration of "idha" with his saying "On Friday" that he deprived it of indicating the condition, which is its predominant meaning. Had it been a conditional, and the apodosis been the sentence introduced by "laysa," the particle "fa" would have been required, unless it is elided in poetry, as that occurs. So we say: "When Zayd treats you well, you will not leave his reward," and it is not permissible to say "lasta" without "fa" except in cases of necessity. As for his assumption, "When it occurs, such and such will happen," it indicates that in his view "idha" is conditional, and for that reason he supposed for it an apodosis that governs it. As for his saying "by implying udhkur," it strips it of being an adverbial and makes it a direct object in the accusative governed by "udhkur."

"Kadhibah": its apparent sense is that it is an active participle from "kadhaba," and it is an adjective of an elided noun. Al-Zamakhshari supposed it to be "nafs kadhibah" (a lying soul), meaning that when it occurs there will be no soul that lies about Allah, or lies in denying the unseen, because at that time every soul will be believing and truthful, whereas most souls today are liars and deniers, according to His saying: ﴿So when they saw Our might, they said: "We believe in Allah alone"﴾ [Ghafir: 84]; ﴿They will not believe in it until they see the painful punishment﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 201]; ﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease to be in doubt about it until the Hour comes upon them﴾ [al-Hajj: 55]. The "lam" is like it in His saying: ﴿Oh, I wish I had sent forth for my life﴾ [al-Fajr: 24], since there will be no soul for it that lies to it and says to it: "You did not lie," as today there are many souls that say to it: "You did not lie." Or it is from their saying: "His soul deceived him in a great matter," when it encourages him to undertake it and says to him: "You can bear it and what is beyond it," so he approaches it without care, in the sense that it is an event that cannot be endured because of its severity and horror, and that no soul at that time will encourage its owner with what it says to him in great matters, and make him think he can bear and endure it, because on that day they will be weaker and more humbled than that. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Like scattered moths﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 4]? Moths are a symbol of weakness. End of quote. It is excessive and verbose.

Ibn Atiyyah supposed it as a circumstantial "hal kadhibah" (a lying state), and said: The statement may have two meanings in this case. One is "kadhibah," meaning something lied about in what is reported concerning it, so it is called a lie for this reason, as you say: "This is a lying story," meaning it is a story in which there is lying. The second is "hal kadhibah," meaning its occurrence will not be delayed, as you say: "Such a one, when he takes on a task, does not fail." Qatadah and al-Hasan said: The meaning is: there is no denial of it, no refusal, and no postponement, so "kadhibah" in this case is a verbal noun, like "al-'aqibah," "al-'afiyah," and "khaizanat al-a'yun" (the treachery of the eyes). The sentence ﴿There will be no denying its occurrence﴾, according to what al-Zamakhshari supposed, that "idha" is governed by "laysa," would be the beginning of the surah, unless it is believed to be the apodosis of "idha," or governed by "udhkur," in which case it would not be the beginning of a speech. Ibn Atiyyah said: It is in the position of a circumstantial clause. What appears to me is that it is a parenthetical sentence between the conditional and its apodosis.

The majority read ﴿khāfiḍatun rāfiʿatun﴾ with both words in the nominative (rafʿ), taking them as predicates of an implied subject, "it is" (hiya). Zayd ibn ʿAlī, al-Ḥasan, ʿĪsā, Abū Ḥaywa, Ibn Abī ʿAbla, Ibn Miqsam, al-Zaʿfarānī, and al-Yazīdī in his own choice of reading, read them with the accusative (naṣb). Ibn Khālawayh said: al-Kisāʾī said, "Had al-Yazīdī not preceded me to it, I would have read it that way." The accusative here is in the position of the circumstantial accusative (ḥāl, a word describing the state of the subject at the time of the action).

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "This comes after the ḥāl that is ﴿laysa li-waqʿatihā kādhibatun﴾ ('no denying its occurrence'). You may also continue the ḥālāt (circumstantial clauses), just as you may continue the predicates (akhbār) of a subject. The first reading is more famous and more striking in meaning, because the position of the ḥāl in speech is the position of something which, if left unmentioned, would be dispensed with, while the position of the clauses that state a fact with certainty is the position of something of concern." End of quotation.

This point that he made was preceded by Abū al-Faḍl al-Rāzī. In Kitāb al-Lawāmiḥ he said: "The one who is in the ḥāl is the event (al-wāqiʿa), and the agent is 'waqaʿat' (it occurred). It is also permissible that ﴿laysa li-waqʿatihā kādhibatun﴾ be another ḥāl of al-wāqiʿa, with the implied sense: 'when the event occurs, truthfully.' These are three ḥālāt of one subject. It is permissible for different ḥālāt to come from one subject, just as different adjectives (nuʿūt) that are opposite to each other, and many predicates (akhbār), may come from one subject. When all of these are taken as ḥālāt, the governing agent of ﴿idhā waqaʿat﴾ ('when it occurs') is omitted, indicated by the context, with the implied sense of 'they will be called to account' or something similar." End of quotation.

The enumeration of the ḥālāt and predicates in this respect is disputed and detailed, and it is discussed in grammar (naḥw). Therefore this is not something on which the grammarians are agreed.

The majority said: On the Day of Resurrection, the heaven, the earth, and the mountains will be torn apart (tanfaṭiru) by it, and this structure will be broken down (tanhaddu) by it, through the raising of some bodies and the lowering of others. It is thus an expression of the intensity of the terror and turmoil.

Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: The Blast (al-ṣayḥa) lowers its force so that those nearest hear it, and raises it so that those farthest hear it.

Qatāda and ʿUthmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Surāqa said: The Resurrection lowers some peoples to the Fire and raises other peoples to the Garden.

Al-Zamakhsharī took these statements, as is his habit, and clothed them in some striking wording. He said: "It raises some peoples and lowers others. Either this describes it as severe, because great events are like that: some people rise to high ranks in them and others are brought low; or the wretched are brought down to the lowest depths (al-darakāt) and the blessed are raised to the degrees (al-darajāt). Or it is that it shakes things from their places, so that it lowers some and raises others, since it casts down the heaven in pieces (kisafan), scatters the stars and causes them to fall, and sets the mountains moving so that they pass through the air like clouds." End of quotation.

Surat al-Waqi'ah is Meccan, and it has ninety-six verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

"Rujjat al-ardu" means the earth was shaken and set in violent motion, to the point that buildings collapse and mountains fall down. "Bussat al-jibal" means they were crumbled to pieces; it was also said they were set moving, from the saying "bassa al-ghanam," meaning he drove the sheep. It is also said that "rujjat al-ardu" and "bussat al-jibal" are intransitive.

"Al-mash'amah" derives from "al-shu'm" (ill omen), or from "the left hand" (al-yad al-shu'ma), which is the left side.

"Al-thullalah" means a group, whether large or small. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Al-ummah" among people is a great multitude. The poet said:

Three Khandaqiyyah came to them, with an army like a flood torrent, foaming.

"Al-mawdunah" means woven with the parts of it fitted one upon another, like the links of a coat of mail. Al-A'sha said:

And of the weaving of Dawud, a mawdunah, moving with the tribe, camel after camel.

From this comes "wadin al-naqah," which is the girth of the she-camel, because it is mawdun, meaning twisted. The reciter said:

Toward you she goes, restless, her girth, with her unborn young lying across her belly.

Her religion opposes the religion of the Christians.

"Al-ibriq" is on the pattern "if'il" from "al-bariq" (gleam); it is a vessel for drinking with a spout. It was said it also has a handle. It is one of the wine vessels among the Arabs. The poet said:

As if their ewer were a gazelle upon a height, its neck bent, daubed with the cloth of cotton, its mouth crushed.

Adi ibn Zayd said:

We call to the morning, and there came a slave-girl with a ewer in her right hand.

"Suddi'a al-qawm bil-khamr" means the people were struck with headache from it. It was also said: "suddi'u" means they were scattered.

"Al-sidr" was discussed earlier in Surat Saba'.

"Al-makhdud" means the one whose thorns have been cut off. Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:

Indeed the gardens in the Paradises are shaded, in them are maidens whose lote-trees are without thorns.

"Al-talh" is the banana tree; it was also said it is a tree of the acacia kind with many thorns.

"Al-maskub" means poured out.

"Al-'arub" means one who is loving toward her husband.

"Al-tirb" means delight. It also refers to one who is born at the same time as another, and both were named so because they touched the dust at the same time. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

Zayd ibn ʿAlī, al-Ḥasan, ʿĪsā, Abū Ḥaywa, Ibn Abī ʿAbla, Ibn Miqsam, al-Zaʿfarānī, and al-Yazīdī in his own choice of reading, read them with the accusative (naṣb). Ibn Khālawayh said: al-Kisāʾī said, "Had al-Yazīdī not preceded me to it, I would have read it that way." The accusative here is in the position of the circumstantial accusative (ḥāl, a word describing the state of the subject at the time of the action).

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "This comes after the ḥāl that is ﴿laysa li-waqʿatihā kādhibatun﴾ ('no denying its occurrence'). You may also continue the ḥālāt (circumstantial clauses), just as you may continue the predicates (akhbār) of a subject. The first reading is more famous and more striking in meaning, because the position of the ḥāl in speech is the position of something which, if left unmentioned, would be dispensed with, while the position of the clauses that state a fact with certainty is the position of something of concern." End of quotation.

This point that he made was preceded by Abū al-Faḍl al-Rāzī. In Kitāb al-Lawāmiḥ he said: "The one who is in the ḥāl is the event (al-wāqiʿa), and the agent is 'waqaʿat' (it occurred). It is also permissible that ﴿laysa li-waqʿatihā kādhibatun﴾ be another ḥāl of al-wāqiʿa, with the implied sense: 'when the event occurs, truthfully.' These are three ḥālāt of one subject. It is permissible for different ḥālāt to come from one subject, just as different adjectives (nuʿūt) that are opposite to each other, and many predicates (akhbār), may come from one subject. When all of these are taken as ḥālāt, the governing agent of ﴿idhā waqaʿat﴾ ('when it occurs') is omitted, indicated by the context, with the implied sense of 'they will be called to account' or something similar." End of quotation.

The enumeration of the ḥālāt and predicates in this respect is disputed and detailed, and it is discussed in grammar (naḥw). Therefore this is not something on which the grammarians are agreed.

The majority said: On the Day of Resurrection, the heaven, the earth, and the mountains will be torn apart (tanfaṭiru) by it, and this structure will be broken down (tanhaddu) by it, through the raising of some bodies and the lowering of others. It is thus an expression of the intensity of the terror and turmoil.

Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: The Blast (al-ṣayḥa) lowers its force so that those nearest hear it, and raises it so that those farthest hear it.

Qatāda and ʿUthmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Surāqa said: The Resurrection lowers some peoples to the Fire and raises other peoples to the Garden.

Al-Zamakhsharī took these statements, as is his habit, and clothed them in some striking wording. He said: "It raises some peoples and lowers others. Either this describes it as severe, because great events are like that: some people rise to high ranks in them and others are brought low; or the wretched are brought down to the lowest depths (al-darakāt) and the blessed are raised to the degrees (al-darajāt). Or it is that it shakes things from their places, so that it lowers some and raises others, since it casts down the heaven in pieces (kisafan), scatters the stars and causes them to fall, and sets the mountains moving so that they pass through the air like clouds." End of quotation.

Surat al-Waqi'ah is Meccan, and it has ninety-six verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

"Rujjat al-ardu" means the earth was shaken and set in violent motion, to the point that buildings collapse and mountains fall down. "Bussat al-jibal" means they were crumbled to pieces; it was also said they were set moving, from the saying "bassa al-ghanam," meaning he drove the sheep. It is also said that "rujjat al-ardu" and "bussat al-jibal" are intransitive.

"Al-mash'amah" derives from "al-shu'm" (ill omen), or from "the left hand" (al-yad al-shu'ma), which is the left side.

"Al-thullalah" means a group, whether large or small. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Al-ummah" among people is a great multitude. The poet said:

Three Khandaqiyyah came to them, with an army like a flood torrent, foaming.

"Al-mawdunah" means woven with the parts of it fitted one upon another, like the links of a coat of mail. Al-A'sha said:

And of the weaving of Dawud, a mawdunah, moving with the tribe, camel after camel.

From this comes "wadin al-naqah," which is the girth of the she-camel, because it is mawdun, meaning twisted. The reciter said:

Toward you she goes, restless, her girth, with her unborn young lying across her belly.

Her religion opposes the religion of the Christians.

"Al-ibriq" is on the pattern "if'il" from "al-bariq" (gleam); it is a vessel for drinking with a spout. It was said it also has a handle. It is one of the wine vessels among the Arabs. The poet said:

As if their ewer were a gazelle upon a height, its neck bent, daubed with the cloth of cotton, its mouth crushed.

Adi ibn Zayd said:

We call to the morning, and there came a slave-girl with a ewer in her right hand.

"Suddi'a al-qawm bil-khamr" means the people were struck with headache from it. It was also said: "suddi'u" means they were scattered.

"Al-sidr" was discussed earlier in Surat Saba'.

"Al-makhdud" means the one whose thorns have been cut off. Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:

Indeed the gardens in the Paradises are shaded, in them are maidens whose lote-trees are without thorns.

"Al-talh" is the banana tree; it was also said it is a tree of the acacia kind with many thorns.

"Al-maskub" means poured out.

"Al-'arub" means one who is loving toward her husband.

"Al-tirb" means delight. It also refers to one who is born at the same time as another, and both were named so because they touched the dust at the same time. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

This surah is Meccan, and its connection to what precedes it is that it includes the punishment of the criminals and the bliss of the believers. He distinguished between the two gardens of some believers and the two gardens of others by His saying: ﴿And besides these two, there are two other gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 62]. Thus the world is divided into disbelievers, lesser believers, and superior believers. Likewise, the opening of this surah describes them as companions of the right hand, companions of the left hand, and the foremost, who are the ones brought near, and the companions of the right hand; and it ends with the deniers.

Ibn Abbas said: "Al-Waqi'ah" is one of the names of the Resurrection, like "al-Sakhkhah," "al-Tammah," and "al-Azifah," and these names indicate the greatness of its matter. The meaning of ﴿When the Event occurs﴾ is: when the one that must occur occurs, as you say: "The event happened," and "what was to be, was." The occurrence of a matter is its descent; it is said: "What I was expecting has occurred," meaning what I was awaiting has come down.

Al-Dahhak said: "Al-Waqi'ah" is the Cry, which is the blast in the Trumpet. It was also said: "Al-Waqi'ah" is the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis, which will fall on the Day of Resurrection.

The governing element of "idha" is the verb after it, as we have established in the books of grammar. It is in a position of genitive by the attachment of "idha" to it, so it needs a supposed governing element, since it is apparent that there is no spoken apodosis that governs it. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "By what is idha in the accusative?" I say: "By laysa (is not), like your saying: 'On Friday, I have no business,' or by an elided element, meaning: when it occurs, such and such will happen; or by implying 'udhkur' (mention)." End of quote.

As for its being in the accusative by "laysa," no grammarian, nor anyone who has a share of the discipline of i'rab (grammatical inflection), goes to such a view, because "laysa" in negation, like "kama" and "ma," does not govern. Likewise "laysa," because "laysa" is stripped of indicating an event and a time. The claim that it is a verb is metaphorical, because the definition of a verb does not apply to it. The governing element of an adverbial of time is only the event that takes place in it: when you say, "I will stand on Friday," standing takes place on Friday, and there is no event in "laysa," so how can it govern the adverbial? The example he compared it to, namely "On the Day of Resurrection, I have no business," does not indicate that "Friday" is accusative by "laysa." Rather, it is accusative by the governing element of the predicate of "laysa," which is the prepositional phrase, so it is a case of fronting the complement of the predicate before "laysa." The fronting of such is based on the permissibility of fronting the predicate of "laysa" before it, which is disputed, and it was not heard from the speech of the Arabs: "Standing, Zayd is not." "Laysa" indicates only the negation of the predicate's judgment about the subject, like "kama," but when pronoun endings attach to it, some people made it a verb, while in reality it is a particle of negation like "ma" (not).

It appears from al-Zamakhshari's illustration of "idha" with his saying "On Friday" that he deprived it of indicating the condition, which is its predominant meaning. Had it been a conditional, and the apodosis been the sentence introduced by "laysa," the particle "fa" would have been required, unless it is elided in poetry, as that occurs. So we say: "When Zayd treats you well, you will not leave his reward," and it is not permissible to say "lasta" without "fa" except in cases of necessity. As for his assumption, "When it occurs, such and such will happen," it indicates that in his view "idha" is conditional, and for that reason he supposed for it an apodosis that governs it. As for his saying "by implying udhkur," it strips it of being an adverbial and makes it a direct object in the accusative governed by "udhkur."

"Kadhibah": its apparent sense is that it is an active participle from "kadhaba," and it is an adjective of an elided noun. Al-Zamakhshari supposed it to be "nafs kadhibah" (a lying soul), meaning that when it occurs there will be no soul that lies about Allah, or lies in denying the unseen, because at that time every soul will be believing and truthful, whereas most souls today are liars and deniers, according to His saying: ﴿So when they saw Our might, they said: "We believe in Allah alone"﴾ [Ghafir: 84]; ﴿They will not believe in it until they see the painful punishment﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 201]; ﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease to be in doubt about it until the Hour comes upon them﴾ [al-Hajj: 55]. The "lam" is like it in His saying: ﴿Oh, I wish I had sent forth for my life﴾ [al-Fajr: 24], since there will be no soul for it that lies to it and says to it: "You did not lie," as today there are many souls that say to it: "You did not lie." Or it is from their saying: "His soul deceived him in a great matter," when it encourages him to undertake it and says to him: "You can bear it and what is beyond it," so he approaches it without care, in the sense that it is an event that cannot be endured because of its severity and horror, and that no soul at that time will encourage its owner with what it says to him in great matters, and make him think he can bear and endure it, because on that day they will be weaker and more humbled than that. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Like scattered moths﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 4]? Moths are a symbol of weakness. End of quote. It is excessive and verbose.

Ibn Atiyyah supposed it as a circumstantial "hal kadhibah" (a lying state), and said: The statement may have two meanings in this case. One is "kadhibah," meaning something lied about in what is reported concerning it, so it is called a lie for this reason, as you say: "This is a lying story," meaning it is a story in which there is lying. The second is "hal kadhibah," meaning its occurrence will not be delayed, as you say: "Such a one, when he takes on a task, does not fail." Qatadah and al-Hasan said: The meaning is: there is no denial of it, no refusal, and no postponement, so "kadhibah" in this case is a verbal noun, like "al-'aqibah," "al-'afiyah," and "khaizanat al-a'yun" (the treachery of the eyes). Toward you she goes, restless, her girth, with her unborn young lying across her belly.

Her religion opposes the religion of the Christians.

"Al-ibriq" is on the pattern "if'il" from "al-bariq" (gleam); it is a vessel for drinking with a spout. It was said it also has a handle. It is one of the wine vessels among the Arabs. The poet said:

As if their ewer were a gazelle upon a height, its neck bent, daubed with the cloth of cotton, its mouth crushed.

Adi ibn Zayd said:

We call to the morning, and there came a slave-girl with a ewer in her right hand.

"Suddi'a al-qawm bil-khamr" means the people were struck with headache from it. It was also said: "suddi'u" means they were scattered.

"Al-sidr" was discussed earlier in Surat Saba'.

Indeed the gardens in the Paradises are shaded, in them are maidens whose lote-trees are without thorns.

"Al-talh" is the banana tree; it was also said it is a tree of the acacia kind with many thorns.

"Al-maskub" means poured out.

"Al-'arub" means one who is loving toward her husband.

"Al-tirb" means delight. It also refers to one who is born at the same time as another, and both were named so because they touched the dust at the same time. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

This surah is Meccan, and its connection to what precedes it is that it includes the punishment of the criminals and the bliss of the believers. He distinguished between the two gardens of some believers and the two gardens of others by His saying: ﴿And besides these two, there are two other gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 62]. Thus the world is divided into disbelievers, lesser believers, and superior believers. Likewise, the opening of this surah describes them as companions of the right hand, companions of the left hand, and the foremost, who are the ones brought near, and the companions of the right hand; and it ends with the deniers.

Ibn Abbas said: "Al-Waqi'ah" is one of the names of the Resurrection, like "al-Sakhkhah," "al-Tammah," and "al-Azifah," and these names indicate the greatness of its matter. The meaning of ﴿When the Event occurs﴾ is: when the one that must occur occurs, as you say: "The event happened," and "what was to be, was." The occurrence of a matter is its descent; it is said: "What I was expecting has occurred," meaning what I was awaiting has come down.

Al-Dahhak said: "Al-Waqi'ah" is the Cry, which is the blast in the Trumpet. It was also said: "Al-Waqi'ah" is the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis, which will fall on the Day of Resurrection.

The governing element of "idha" is the verb after it, as we have established in the books of grammar. It is in a position of genitive by the attachment of "idha" to it, so it needs a supposed governing element, since it is apparent that there is no spoken apodosis that governs it. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "By what is idha in the accusative?" I say: "By laysa (is not), like your saying: 'On Friday, I have no business,' or by an elided element, meaning: when it occurs, such and such will happen; or by implying 'udhkur' (mention)." End of quote.

As for its being in the accusative by "laysa," no grammarian, nor anyone who has a share of the discipline of i'rab (grammatical inflection), goes to such a view, because "laysa" in negation, like "kama" and "ma," does not govern. Likewise "laysa," because "laysa" is stripped of indicating an event and a time. The claim that it is a verb is metaphorical, because the definition of a verb does not apply to it. The governing element of an adverbial of time is only the event that takes place in it: when you say, "I will stand on Friday," standing takes place on Friday, and there is no event in "laysa," so how can it govern the adverbial? The example he compared it to, namely "On the Day of Resurrection, I have no business," does not indicate that "Friday" is accusative by "laysa." Rather, it is accusative by the governing element of the predicate of "laysa," which is the prepositional phrase, so it is a case of fronting the complement of the predicate before "laysa." The fronting of such is based on the permissibility of fronting the predicate of "laysa" before it, which is disputed, and it was not heard from the speech of the Arabs: "Standing, Zayd is not." "Laysa" indicates only the negation of the predicate's judgment about the subject, like "kama," but when pronoun endings attach to it, some people made it a verb, while in reality it is a particle of negation like "ma" (not).

It appears from al-Zamakhshari's illustration of "idha" with his saying "On Friday" that he deprived it of indicating the condition, which is its predominant meaning. Had it been a conditional, and the apodosis been the sentence introduced by "laysa," the particle "fa" would have been required, unless it is elided in poetry, as that occurs. So we say: "When Zayd treats you well, you will not leave his reward," and it is not permissible to say "lasta" without "fa" except in cases of necessity. As for his assumption, "When it occurs, such and such will happen," it indicates that in his view "idha" is conditional, and for that reason he supposed for it an apodosis that governs it. As for his saying "by implying udhkur," it strips it of being an adverbial and makes it a direct object in the accusative governed by "udhkur."

"Kadhibah": its apparent sense is that it is an active participle from "kadhaba," and it is an adjective of an elided noun. Al-Zamakhshari supposed it to be "nafs kadhibah" (a lying soul), meaning that when it occurs there will be no soul that lies about Allah, or lies in denying the unseen, because at that time every soul will be believing and truthful, whereas most souls today are liars and deniers, according to His saying: ﴿So when they saw Our might, they said: "We believe in Allah alone"﴾ [Ghafir: 84]; ﴿They will not believe in it until they see the painful punishment﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 201]; ﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease to be in doubt about it until the Hour comes upon them﴾ [al-Hajj: 55]. The "lam" is like it in His saying: ﴿Oh, I wish I had sent forth for my life﴾ [al-Fajr: 24], since there will be no soul for it that lies to it and says to it: "You did not lie," as today there are many souls that say to it: "You did not lie." Or it is from their saying: "His soul deceived him in a great matter," when it encourages him to undertake it and says to him: "You can bear it and what is beyond it," so he approaches it without care, in the sense that it is an event that cannot be endured because of its severity and horror, and that no soul at that time will encourage its owner with what it says to him in great matters, and make him think he can bear and endure it, because on that day they will be weaker and more humbled than that. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Like scattered moths﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 4]? Moths are a symbol of weakness. End of quote. It is excessive and verbose.

Ibn Atiyyah supposed it as a circumstantial "hal kadhibah" (a lying state), and said: The statement may have two meanings in this case. One is "kadhibah," meaning something lied about in what is reported concerning it, so it is called a lie for this reason, as you say: "This is a lying story," meaning it is a story in which there is lying. The second is "hal kadhibah," meaning its occurrence will not be delayed, as you say: "Such a one, when he takes on a task, does not fail." Qatadah and al-Hasan said: The meaning is: there is no denial of it, no refusal, and no postponement, so "kadhibah" in this case is a verbal noun, like "al-'aqibah," "al-'afiyah," and "khaizanat al-a'yun" (the treachery of the eyes). The sentence ﴿There will be no denying its occurrence﴾, according to what al-Zamakhshari supposed, that "idha" is governed by "laysa," would be the beginning of the surah, unless it is believed to be the apodosis of "idha," or governed by "udhkur," in which case it would not be the beginning of a speech. Ibn Atiyyah said: It is in the position of a circumstantial clause. What appears to me is that it is a parenthetical sentence between the conditional and its apodosis.

The majority read ﴿khāfiḍatun rāfiʿatun﴾ with both words in the nominative (rafʿ), taking them as predicates of an implied subject, "it is" (hiya). Zayd ibn ʿAlī, al-Ḥasan, ʿĪsā, Abū Ḥaywa, Ibn Abī ʿAbla, Ibn Miqsam, al-Zaʿfarānī, and al-Yazīdī in his own choice of reading, read them with the accusative (naṣb). Ibn Khālawayh said: al-Kisāʾī said, "Had al-Yazīdī not preceded me to it, I would have read it that way." The accusative here is in the position of the circumstantial accusative (ḥāl, a word describing the state of the subject at the time of the action).

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "This comes after the ḥāl that is ﴿laysa li-waqʿatihā kādhibatun﴾ ('no denying its occurrence'). You may also continue the ḥālāt (circumstantial clauses), just as you may continue the predicates (akhbār) of a subject. The first reading is more famous and more striking in meaning, because the position of the ḥāl in speech is the position of something which, if left unmentioned, would be dispensed with, while the position of the clauses that state a fact with certainty is the position of something of concern." End of quotation.

This point that he made was preceded by Abū al-Faḍl al-Rāzī. In Kitāb al-Lawāmiḥ he said: "The one who is in the ḥāl is the event (al-wāqiʿa), and the agent is 'waqaʿat' (it occurred). It is also permissible that ﴿laysa li-waqʿatihā kādhibatun﴾ be another ḥāl of al-wāqiʿa, with the implied sense: 'when the event occurs, truthfully.' These are three ḥālāt of one subject. It is permissible for different ḥālāt to come from one subject, just as different adjectives (nuʿūt) that are opposite to each other, and many predicates (akhbār), may come from one subject. When all of these are taken as ḥālāt, the governing agent of ﴿idhā waqaʿat﴾ ('when it occurs') is omitted, indicated by the context, with the implied sense of 'they will be called to account' or something similar." End of quotation.

The enumeration of the ḥālāt and predicates in this respect is disputed and detailed, and it is discussed in grammar (naḥw). Therefore this is not something on which the grammarians are agreed.

The majority said: On the Day of Resurrection, the heaven, the earth, and the mountains will be torn apart (tanfaṭiru) by it, and this structure will be broken down (tanhaddu) by it, through the raising of some bodies and the lowering of others. It is thus an expression of the intensity of the terror and turmoil.

Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: The Blast (al-ṣayḥa) lowers its force so that those nearest hear it, and raises it so that those farthest hear it.

Qatāda and ʿUthmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Surāqa said: The Resurrection lowers some peoples to the Fire and raises other peoples to the Garden.

Al-Zamakhsharī took these statements, as is his habit, and clothed them in some striking wording. He said: "It raises some peoples and lowers others. Either this describes it as severe, because great events are like that: some people rise to high ranks in them and others are brought low; or the wretched are brought down to the lowest depths (al-darakāt) and the blessed are raised to the degrees (al-darajāt). Or it is that it shakes things from their places, so that it lowers some and raises others, since it casts down the heaven in pieces (kisafan), scatters the stars and causes them to fall, and sets the mountains moving so that they pass through the air like clouds." End of quotation.

Surat al-Waqi'ah is Meccan, and it has ninety-six verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Three Khandaqiyyah came to them, with an army like a flood torrent, foaming.

As for his assumption, "When it occurs, such and such will happen," it indicates that in his view "idha" is conditional, and for that reason he supposed for it an apodosis that governs it. As for his saying "by implying udhkur," it strips it of being an adverbial and makes it a direct object in the accusative governed by "udhkur."

"Kadhibah": its apparent sense is that it is an active participle from "kadhaba," and it is an adjective of an elided noun. Al-Zamakhshari supposed it to be "nafs kadhibah" (a lying soul), meaning that when it occurs there will be no soul that lies about Allah, or lies in denying the unseen, because at that time every soul will be believing and truthful, whereas most souls today are liars and deniers, according to His saying: ﴿So when they saw Our might, they said: "We believe in Allah alone"﴾ [Ghafir: 84]; ﴿They will not believe in it until they see the painful punishment﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 201]; ﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease to be in doubt about it until the Hour comes upon them﴾ [al-Hajj: 55]. The "lam" is like it in His saying: ﴿Oh, I wish I had sent forth for my life﴾ [al-Fajr: 24], since there will be no soul for it that lies to it and says to it: "You did not lie," as today there are many souls that say to it: "You did not lie." Or it is from their saying: "His soul deceived him in a great matter," when it encourages him to undertake it and says to him: "You can bear it and what is beyond it," so he approaches it without care, in the sense that it is an event that cannot be endured because of its severity and horror, and that no soul at that time will encourage its owner with what it says to him in great matters, and make him think he can bear and endure it, because on that day they will be weaker and more humbled than that. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Like scattered moths﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 4]? Moths are a symbol of weakness. End of quote. It is excessive and verbose.

Ibn Atiyyah supposed it as a circumstantial "hal kadhibah" (a lying state), and said: The statement may have two meanings in this case. One is "kadhibah," meaning something lied about in what is reported concerning it, so it is called a lie for this reason, as you say: "This is a lying story," meaning it is a story in which there is lying. The second is "hal kadhibah," meaning its occurrence will not be delayed, as you say: "Such a one, when he takes on a task, does not fail." Qatadah and al-Hasan said: The meaning is: there is no denial of it, no refusal, and no postponement, so "kadhibah" in this case is a verbal noun, like "al-'aqibah," "al-'afiyah," and "khaizanat al-a'yun" (the treachery of the eyes). The sentence ﴿There will be no denying its occurrence﴾, according to what al-Zamakhshari supposed, that "idha" is governed by "laysa," would be the beginning of the surah, unless it is believed to be the apodosis of "idha," or governed by "udhkur," in which case it would not be the beginning of a speech. Ibn Atiyyah said: It is in the position of a circumstantial clause. What appears to me is that it is a parenthetical sentence between the conditional and its apodosis.

The majority read ﴿khāfiḍatun rāfiʿatun﴾ with both words in the nominative (rafʿ), taking them as predicates of an implied subject, "it is" (hiya). Zayd ibn ʿAlī, al-Ḥasan, ʿĪsā, Abū Ḥaywa, Ibn Abī ʿAbla, Ibn Miqsam, al-Zaʿfarānī, and al-Yazīdī in his own choice of reading, read them with the accusative (naṣb). Ibn Khālawayh said: al-Kisāʾī said, "Had al-Yazīdī not preceded me to it, I would have read it that way." The accusative here is in the position of the circumstantial accusative (ḥāl, a word describing the state of the subject at the time of the action).

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "This comes after the ḥāl that is ﴿laysa li-waqʿatihā kādhibatun﴾ ('no denying its occurrence'). You may also continue the ḥālāt (circumstantial clauses), just as you may continue the predicates (akhbār) of a subject. The first reading is more famous and more striking in meaning, because the position of the ḥāl in speech is the position of something which, if left unmentioned, would be dispensed with, while the position of the clauses that state a fact with certainty is the position of something of concern." End of quotation.

This point that he made was preceded by Abū al-Faḍl al-Rāzī. In Kitāb al-Lawāmiḥ he said: "The one who is in the ḥāl is the event (al-wāqiʿa), and the agent is 'waqaʿat' (it occurred). It is also permissible that ﴿laysa li-waqʿatihā kādhibatun﴾ be another ḥāl of al-wāqiʿa, with the implied sense: 'when the event occurs, truthfully.' These are three ḥālāt of one subject. It is permissible for different ḥālāt to come from one subject, just as different adjectives (nuʿūt) that are opposite to each other, and many predicates (akhbār), may come from one subject. When all of these are taken as ḥālāt, the governing agent of ﴿idhā waqaʿat﴾ ('when it occurs') is omitted, indicated by the context, with the implied sense of 'they will be called to account' or something similar." End of quotation.

The enumeration of the ḥālāt and predicates in this respect is disputed and detailed, and it is discussed in grammar (naḥw). Therefore this is not something on which the grammarians are agreed.

The majority said: On the Day of Resurrection, the heaven, the earth, and the mountains will be torn apart (tanfaṭiru) by it, and this structure will be broken down (tanhaddu) by it, through the raising of some bodies and the lowering of others. It is thus an expression of the intensity of the terror and turmoil.

Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: The Blast (al-ṣayḥa) lowers its force so that those nearest hear it, and raises it so that those farthest hear it.

Qatāda and ʿUthmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Surāqa said: The Resurrection lowers some peoples to the Fire and raises other peoples to the Garden.

Al-Zamakhsharī took these statements, as is his habit, and clothed them in some striking wording. He said: "It raises some peoples and lowers others. Either this describes it as severe, because great events are like that: some people rise to high ranks in them and others are brought low; or the wretched are brought down to the lowest depths (al-darakāt) and the blessed are raised to the degrees (al-darajāt). Or it is that it shakes things from their places, so that it lowers some and raises others, since it casts down the heaven in pieces (kisafan), scatters the stars and causes them to fall, and sets the mountains moving so that they pass through the air like clouds." End of quotation.

Surat al-Waqi'ah is Meccan, and it has ninety-six verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

"Rujjat al-ardu" means the earth was shaken and set in violent motion, to the point that buildings collapse and mountains fall down. "Bussat al-jibal" means they were crumbled to pieces; it was also said they were set moving, from the saying "bassa al-ghanam," meaning he drove the sheep. It is also said that "rujjat al-ardu" and "bussat al-jibal" are intransitive.

"Al-mash'amah" derives from "al-shu'm" (ill omen), or from "the left hand" (al-yad al-shu'ma), which is the left side.

"Al-thullalah" means a group, whether large or small. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Al-ummah" among people is a great multitude. The poet said:

Three Khandaqiyyah came to them, with an army like a flood torrent, foaming.

"Al-mawdunah" means woven with the parts of it fitted one upon another, like the links of a coat of mail. Al-A'sha said:

And of the weaving of Dawud, a mawdunah, moving with the tribe, camel after camel.

From this comes "wadin al-naqah," which is the girth of the she-camel, because it is mawdun, meaning twisted. The reciter said:

Toward you she goes, restless, her girth, with her unborn young lying across her belly.

Her religion opposes the religion of the Christians.

"Al-ibriq" is on the pattern "if'il" from "al-bariq" (gleam); it is a vessel for drinking with a spout. It was said it also has a handle. It is one of the wine vessels among the Arabs. The poet said:

As if their ewer were a gazelle upon a height, its neck bent, daubed with the cloth of cotton, its mouth crushed.

Adi ibn Zayd said:

We call to the morning, and there came a slave-girl with a ewer in her right hand.

"Suddi'a al-qawm bil-khamr" means the people were struck with headache from it. It was also said: "suddi'u" means they were scattered.

"Al-sidr" was discussed earlier in Surat Saba'.

"Al-makhdud" means the one whose thorns have been cut off. Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:

Indeed the gardens in the Paradises are shaded, in them are maidens whose lote-trees are without thorns.

"Al-talh" is the banana tree; it was also said it is a tree of the acacia kind with many thorns.

"Al-maskub" means poured out.

"Al-'arub" means one who is loving toward her husband.

"Al-tirb" means delight. It also refers to one who is born at the same time as another, and both were named so because they touched the dust at the same time. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

This surah is Meccan, and its connection to what precedes it is that it includes the punishment of the criminals and the bliss of the believers. He distinguished between the two gardens of some believers and the two gardens of others by His saying: ﴿And besides these two, there are two other gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 62]. Thus the world is divided into disbelievers, lesser believers, and superior believers. Likewise, the opening of this surah describes them as companions of the right hand, companions of the left hand, and the foremost, who are the ones brought near, and the companions of the right hand; and it ends with the deniers.

Ibn Abbas said: "Al-Waqi'ah" is one of the names of the Resurrection, like "al-Sakhkhah," "al-Tammah," and "al-Azifah," and these names indicate the greatness of its matter. The meaning of ﴿When the Event occurs﴾ is: when the one that must occur occurs, as you say: "The event happened," and "what was to be, was." The occurrence of a matter is its descent; it is said: "What I was expecting has occurred," meaning what I was awaiting has come down.

Al-Dahhak said: "Al-Waqi'ah" is the Cry, which is the blast in the Trumpet. It was also said: "Al-Waqi'ah" is the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis, which will fall on the Day of Resurrection.

The governing element of "idha" is the verb after it, as we have established in the books of grammar. It is in a position of genitive by the attachment of "idha" to it, so it needs a supposed governing element, since it is apparent that there is no spoken apodosis that governs it. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "By what is idha in the accusative?" I say: "By laysa (is not), like your saying: 'On Friday, I have no business,' or by an elided element, meaning: when it occurs, such and such will happen; or by implying 'udhkur' (mention)." End of quote.

As for its being in the accusative by "laysa," no grammarian, nor anyone who has a share of the discipline of i'rab (grammatical inflection), goes to such a view, because "laysa" in negation, like "kama" and "ma," does not govern. Likewise "laysa," because "laysa" is stripped of indicating an event and a time. The claim that it is a verb is metaphorical, because the definition of a verb does not apply to it. The governing element of an adverbial of time is only the event that takes place in it: when you say, "I will stand on Friday," standing takes place on Friday, and there is no event in "laysa," so how can it govern the adverbial? The example he compared it to, namely "On the Day of Resurrection, I have no business," does not indicate that "Friday" is accusative by "laysa." Rather, it is accusative by the governing element of the predicate of "laysa," which is the prepositional phrase, so it is a case of fronting the complement of the predicate before "laysa." The fronting of such is based on the permissibility of fronting the predicate of "laysa" before it, which is disputed, and it was not heard from the speech of the Arabs: "Standing, Zayd is not." "Laysa" indicates only the negation of the predicate's judgment about the subject, like "kama," but when pronoun endings attach to it, some people made it a verb, while in reality it is a particle of negation like "ma" (not).

It appears from al-Zamakhshari's illustration of "idha" with his saying "On Friday" that he deprived it of indicating the condition, which is its predominant meaning. Had it been a conditional, and the apodosis been the sentence introduced by "laysa," the particle "fa" would have been required, unless it is elided in poetry, as that occurs. So we say: "When Zayd treats you well, you will not leave his reward," and it is not permissible to say "lasta" without "fa" except in cases of necessity.
