There is no contradiction between His saying ﴿and a company of the later generations﴾ and His saying earlier ﴿and few of the later generations﴾, because His saying ﴿of the later generations﴾ refers to the foremost, and His saying ﴿and a company of the later generations﴾ refers to the companions of the right.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 56, verse 8–40 (part 1 of 2):

﴿When the earth is shaken with a violent shaking﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 4]. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was convulsed and set in motion by a pull. He also said, together with 'Ikrimah and Mujahid, that (bussat) means: it was crumbled to dust. It was also said: it was set moving. Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﴿rujjat﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 4] and (bassat) in the active voice. (﴿Idha rujjat﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 4]) is a substitute for ﴿Idha waqa'at﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 1]. In my view the answer of the conditional is pronounced explicitly, namely His saying ﴿then the companions of the right hand﴾, and the meaning is: when such and such occurs, then the companions of the right hand — how happy they are, and how great is the reward they will receive. That is, their happiness and the greatness of their rank with Allah will become manifest at that severe and difficult time for the world. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that it be in the accusative governed by "lowering and raising" (khafidhah rafi'ah), i.e., it lowers and raises at the time the earth is shaken and the mountains are crumbled, because at that time what is high is lowered and what is low is raised. End of quotation. It is not permissible for it to be governed by both of them together; rather by one of them, since two governing agents cannot act upon one effect. Ibn Jinni and Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: ﴿Idha rujjat﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 4] is in the place of nominative, as a predicate of the subject which is ﴿Idha waqa'at﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 1]; neither of them is conditional, rather (idha) is used in the sense of "time," and what follows idha are three states. The meaning: the time of the occurrence of the Event, when it truly occurs, lowering some people and raising others, is the time the earth is shaken. Likewise Ibn Malik claimed that idha may be a subject, and he took this as evidence. We have mentioned in our commentary on al-Tashil what keeps idha within its signification of the conditional, and the explanation of (al-habaa') has already been given in surah al-Furqan.
﴿Munbaththan﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 6]: scattered. Written with two dots (munbattan) in place of the three-dotted thā', the reading of the majority, i.e., cut off.
(And you were): an address to the world, ﴿three kinds﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 7]: three categories. These are the ranks of people on the Day of Resurrection.
﴿Then the companions of the right hand﴾: al-Hasan and al-Rabi' said: they are the blessed ones with respect to themselves. It was said: those who are given their records in their right hands. It was said: the people of lofty rank, as you say: "he is to me on the right" (bil-yamin). It was said: those who are taken to the right side, or the right side of Adam mentioned in the event of the Night Journey, in the black figures.
﴿And the companions of the left hand﴾: they are those who oppose the companions of the right hand in these sayings. Here "companions" (ashab) is the subject, "what" (ma) is a second subject interrogative in the sense of magnification, and "companions of the right hand" is the predicate of "what," and what follows it is the predicate of "companions." The sentence is linked to the subject by repeating the subject with its wording, which most often occurs in contexts of awe and magnification. "What" expresses wonder at the state of the two groups in happiness and wretchedness; the meaning is: what a state they are in.
﴿And the foremost, the foremost﴾: they permitted that it be a subject and predicate, like the saying "you are you" and the verse "I am Abu al-Najm" and "my poetry is my poetry," meaning: those who excelled in precedence, i.e., in acts of obedience, and excelled in them, and whose state is known. And that "the foremost" be an emphatic repetition, with the predicate following that. And that "the foremost" be the subject, with the predicate following it, and you stop at his saying "and the foremost"; and that the object of the first precedence differ from the second precedence: the foremost to faith are the foremost to Paradise. On this view they permitted that "the foremost" be the predicate of his saying "and the foremost," and that it be an attribute with the predicate following. The first view: Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Sibawayh's view is that "the foremost" is the predicate of the subject, meaning the predicate of "and the foremost," and this is like saying "the people, the people," or "you, you," and this is for the sake of magnifying and exalting the matter. End of quotation. This view is favored by the fact that He mentioned the companions of the right hand, marveling at their happiness, and the companions of the left hand, marveling at their wretchedness, so it fits that He mention the foremost, affirming their state in a magnifying manner, by informing that they are at the utmost in greatness and happiness. "The foremost" is general in precedence to acts of obedience and to abandoning sins. 'Uthman ibn Abi Sawdah said: the foremost to the mosques. Ibn Sirin said: they are those who prayed toward both qiblahs. Ka'b said: they are the people of the Qur'an. And in a hadith: "He was asked about the foremost, and he said: they are those who, when given the truth, accept it, and when asked for it, they give it, and they judge people by the judgment they apply to themselves."
(Ulā'ika): a reference to the foremost, the drawn-near, whose ranks are high and whose degrees in Paradise are close to the Throne. The majority read ﴿fi jannat﴾ in the plural; Talhah read "fi jannah" in the singular. He divided the foremost, the drawn-near, into ﴿a multitude from the earlier peoples and a few from the later peoples﴾. Al-Hasan said: the foremost are from the nations, and the foremost are from this community. 'A'ishah said: the two groups exist in every prophet's nation: at its beginning is a multitude, and at its end a few. It was said: they are the prophets, peace be upon them, who were at the beginning of the world, and at its end fewer. And in a hadith: "The two groups are in my community: the foremost at the beginning of the community is a multitude, and the foremost of its remainder until the Day of Resurrection is a few." And "a multitude" is in the nominative by supposing them (ارتفع ثلة على إضمارهم).
The majority read ﴿on thrones﴾ with a dammah on the rā'; Zayd ibn 'Ali and Abu al-Sammal read it with a fatha, a dialect of some Banu Tamim and Kalb, who pronounce the 'ayn of fu'ul, the plural of the doubled fa'il, with a fatha, as in sarir; this was mentioned in al-Saffat.
﴿Mawdunah﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 15]: Ibn 'Abbas said: interwoven with gold. 'Ikrimah said: interlaced with pearls and rubies.
﴿Reclining upon them﴾: that is, upon the thrones; "reclining" is a circumstantial state of the pronoun hidden in ﴿on thrones﴾; (facing one another): each looks at the other. They are described with good companionship, refinement of character, and the purity of their inner selves from rancor, as brothers.
﴿There will circulate among them young boys made eternal﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 17]: they are described as eternal, though everyone in Paradise is eternal, to show that they remain forever in the age of youth, not aging nor changing from the form of youthful bloom. Mujahid said: they do not die. Al-Farra' said: adorned with earrings of the kind called khaladat, which are types of earrings.
﴿And a cup from a flowing spring﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 18]: he said: of wine flowing, running, and streaming.
﴿They will not be stupefied by it﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 19]: most said: the headache that comes from the wine of this world does not reach their heads. I read to our teacher, the eminent scholar Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah have mercy on him, the words of 'Alqamah describing wine:
"It cures headache, and its pourer does not harm you, nor does a dizziness enter the head."
He said: this is a description of the people of Paradise. It was also said: they are not separated from it, meaning: their pleasure is not cut off from them by any cause, as the wine of this world separates its people in various ways of separation, as in the saying: "so the cloud split (tasadda'a) from the city," i.e., it dispersed. Mujahid read "la yassaddda'una" with a fatha on the yā' and a shadda on the ṣād, its original form being yatasaddda'una, the tā' assimilated into the ṣād: i.e., they will not disperse, like His saying: ﴿on that day they will be split apart﴾ [al-Rum: 43]. The majority read with a ḍammah on the yā' and a light ṣād. The majority read "and fruit" and "and meat" in the genitive; Zayd ibn 'Ali read them in the nominative, meaning: and for them. The majority read ﴿nor will they be drained﴾ in the passive. Mujahid, Qatadah, Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: their minds do not depart through intoxication. Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with a fatha on the yā' and a kasra on the zāy, from nazafa the well: he drained its water; the meaning: their wine will not run out. Ibn Abi Ishaq also, 'Abdullah, al-Sulami, al-Jahdari, al-A'mash, Talhah and 'Isa read it with a ḍammah on the yā' and a kasra on the zāy: i.e., their drink will not be exhausted. ﴿From what they choose﴾: they take its best and finest. ﴿From what they desire﴾: i.e., what they wish for.
The majority read ﴿and houris with wide, lovely eyes﴾ in the nominative; 'Ali explained it as being conjoined to "young boys," or to the hidden pronoun in "reclining," or to an omitted subject with its predicate, the estimate being: for them is all this, ﴿and houris with wide, lovely eyes﴾, or with only the predicate omitted: i.e., and for them are houris, or in them are houris. Al-Sulami, al-Hasan, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, al-A'mash, Talhah, al-Mufaddal, Aban, 'Isma and al-Kisa'i read them in the genitive; al-Nakha'i read "wa-hiyar 'in" with the wāw changed to yā' and both in the genitive; the genitive is conjoined to the preceding genitive, meaning: young boys go around them with such and such and with houris with wide, lovely eyes. It was also said: it means: they are blessed with all this and with houris with wide, lovely eyes. Al-Zamakhshari said: conjoined to "gardens of bliss," as if he said: they are in gardens, fruit, meat and houris. End of quotation. This has remoteness and breaks up a speech whose parts are linked to one another; it is a non-Arabic understanding. Ubayy and 'Abdullah read "wa-hūran 'īnan" in the accusative, and they said: on the meaning of "and they are given all this and houris with wide, lovely eyes." Qatadah read "wa-ḥūru 'īnin" in the nominative, annexed to "'īn"; Ibn Miqsam read it in the accusative, annexed to "'īn"; 'Ikrimah read "wa-ḥawrā' 'ayna'" in the singular as a noun of genus, and with a fatha on the hamza in both; it may be genitive, conjoined to the preceding genitive, or accusative, like the reading of Ubayy and 'Abdullah, "wa-ḥūran 'īnan."

He described the pearl as "hidden" (maknun), because it is purest and furthest from change. In a hadith: "Their purity is like the purity of the pearl that no hand has touched." Allah said: ﴿as if they were hidden eggs﴾ [al-Saffat: 49]. A poet, describing a woman as chaste and unexposed to wear, likened her to a hidden pearl in its shell, saying:
"She stood displaying herself between the two curtains of a veil, like the sun on the day of its rising amid the stars.
Or a pearl of the Sadaf sea, whose diver is delighted; when he sees it, he rejoices and prostrates."

﴿A reward for what they used to do﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 24]: it is narrated that the dwellings and the divisions in Paradise are according to the measure of deeds, but entry into Paradise itself is by the mercy and grace of Allah, not by the deed of any doer; and in it is the clear, sound text: "No one will enter Paradise by his deeds." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His grace and mercy."

(Laghwan): idle talk and its vulgarity; ﴿nor sinful speech﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 25]: anything that makes anyone sinful. The apparent view is that ﴿except the word "Peace, peace"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 26] is a disjunctive exception, because it does not fall under idle talk or sin; the view of those who say it is a connected exception is remote. As for "salaman" (peace), al-Zajjaj said: it is a verbal noun whose accusative is governed by "qilan" (speech), i.e., one says to another "salaman salaman." It was said: it is accusative by an omitted verb, which is the governing element of "qilan," i.e., "say: be at peace, peace." It was said: "salaman" is a substitute for "qilan." It was said: it is an attribute of "qilan" by the verbal noun, as if it were said: except a speech free from these defects.

﴿Among lote trees without thorns﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 28]: in Paradise is a tree of its own kind, having fruit like the jars of Hajar, good in taste and fragrance.
﴿Makhdud﴾: free of thorns. Mujahid said: makhdud is the one laden so heavily that its branches bend from the abundance of its fruit, from khadada al-ghusn when he bent it.
The majority read ﴿and banana trees﴾ with a ḥā'; 'Ali, Ja'far ibn Muhammad and 'Abdullah read it with an 'ayn, which he recited from the pulpit. 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' and Mujahid said: ṭalḥ is the banana. al-Hasan said: it is not the banana, but a tree whose shade is cool and moist. It was said: the tree of Umm Ghaylan, which has abundant, fragrant blossom. al-Suddi said: a tree resembling the ṭalḥ of this world, but its fruit is sweeter than honey. Manḍud: that which is arranged from its base to its top, so that no trunk appears.
﴿And extended shade﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 30]: that does not contract, but spreads out and is not abrogated by anything. Mujahid said: this shade is from its lote trees and its ṭalḥ trees.
﴿And water poured out﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 31]: Sufyan and others said: flowing without ditches. It was said: running freely, requiring no labor with a water-wheel or a bucket.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 56, verse 8–40 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Neither cut off﴾: that is, it is perpetual, never cut off at certain times as the fruit of this world is. ﴿Nor forbidden﴾: that is, one is not prevented from partaking of it in any way, and it is not forbidden to them as those in this world are.

It was also read as "wa-fakihatun kathirah" with both words in the nominative (marfu'an), meaning "and there is abundant fruit" [i.e., there is fruit there]. And "wa-furush" is the plural of firash. The majority (al-Jumhur) read it with a dammah on the ra' (furush); Abu Haywah read it with a sukun, marfu'ah, meaning they were arranged until they were raised up, or they were raised upon the beds. The apparent meaning is that the firash is that which is spread out for sitting upon and sleeping on.

Abu 'Ubaydah and others said: the intended meaning of "furush" is the women, because a woman is referred to by the firash, and [God] raised them in value and station. The pronoun in ﴿anshanahunna﴾ refers, in the view of Abu 'Ubaydah, to the furush, since they are the women in his view; and [according to what is indicated by the furush] if what is meant by the furush is the apparent meaning of what they indicate of the garments that are spread out and reclined upon. That is, We began their creation as a new beginning, without birth. The apparent meaning of al-insha' (the bringing into being) is the origination that was not preceded by creation, and this would be specific to the hur (the maidens of paradise) who are not of the offspring of Adam. It is possible that it means the re-creation (insha' al-i'adah), in which case it would apply to the daughters of Adam.

﴿So We made them virgins, 'uruban﴾: al-'Urub. Ibn 'Abbas said: al-'Urub are those who are loving toward their husbands; this was also said by al-Hasan. Ibn 'Abbas also described them as al-'awashiq (the ardent lovers), and from this is the verse of Labid:

"And among the curtains are 'urub, not lewd, / fragrant of hips, whose sight is veiled beyond them."

Ibn Zayd said: al-'Urub are those who beautify speech.

Hamzah and a group including Shuja', 'Abbas, and al-Asma'i (from Abu 'Amr), and a group including Kharijah, Kardam and Abu Khulayd (from Nafi'), and a group including Abu Bakr, Hammad and Aban (from 'Asim), read it with a sukun on the ra' (ʿurban), which is the dialect of Tamim; the rest of the seven read it with a dammah. (Atraban) [means] of the same form and stature. Whoever went to the view that the pronoun in ﴿anshanahunna﴾ refers to the maidens of paradise mentioned before was far off the mark, because that is a story already concluded, namely the story of the foremost (al-sabiqun), and this is the story of the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin). The lam in (li-ashab) is connected to anshanahunna.

﴿A company of the earlier generations﴾: that is, of the past nations, ﴿and a company of the later generations﴾: that is, of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). There is no contradiction between His saying ﴿and a company of the later generations﴾ and His saying earlier ﴿and few of the later generations﴾, because His saying ﴿of the later generations﴾ refers to the foremost, and His saying ﴿and a company of the later generations﴾ refers to the companions of the right.

Al-Sulami, al-Hasan, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, al-A'mash, Talhah, al-Mufaddal, Aban, 'Isma and al-Kisa'i read them in the genitive; al-Nakha'i read "wa-hiyar 'in" with the wāw changed to yā' and both in the genitive; the genitive is conjoined to the preceding genitive, meaning: young boys go around them with such and such and with houris with wide, lovely eyes. It was also said: it means: they are blessed with all this and with houris with wide, lovely eyes. Al-Zamakhshari said: conjoined to "gardens of bliss," as if he said: they are in gardens, fruit, meat and houris. End of quotation. This has remoteness and breaks up a speech whose parts are linked to one another; it is a non-Arabic understanding. Ubayy and 'Abdullah read "wa-hūran 'īnan" in the accusative, and they said: on the meaning of "and they are given all this and houris with wide, lovely eyes." Qatadah read "wa-ḥūru 'īnin" in the nominative, annexed to "'īn"; Ibn Miqsam read it in the accusative, annexed to "'īn"; 'Ikrimah read "wa-ḥawrā' 'ayna'" in the singular as a noun of genus, and with a fatha on the hamza in both; it may be genitive, conjoined to the preceding genitive, or accusative, like the reading of Ubayy and 'Abdullah, "wa-ḥūran 'īnan."

He described the pearl as "hidden" (maknun), because it is purest and furthest from change. In a hadith: "Their purity is like the purity of the pearl that no hand has touched." Allah said: ﴿as if they were hidden eggs﴾ [al-Saffat: 49]. A poet, describing a woman as chaste and unexposed to wear, likened her to a hidden pearl in its shell, saying:
"She stood displaying herself between the two curtains of a veil, like the sun on the day of its rising amid the stars.
Or a pearl of the Sadaf sea, whose diver is delighted; when he sees it, he rejoices and prostrates."

﴿A reward for what they used to do﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 24]: it is narrated that the dwellings and the divisions in Paradise are according to the measure of deeds, but entry into Paradise itself is by the mercy and grace of Allah, not by the deed of any doer; and in it is the clear, sound text: "No one will enter Paradise by his deeds." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His grace and mercy."

(Laghwan): idle talk and its vulgarity; ﴿nor sinful speech﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 25]: anything that makes anyone sinful. The apparent view is that ﴿except the word "Peace, peace"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 26] is a disjunctive exception, because it does not fall under idle talk or sin; the view of those who say it is a connected exception is remote. As for "salaman" (peace), al-Zajjaj said: it is a verbal noun whose accusative is governed by "qilan" (speech), i.e., one says to another "salaman salaman." It was said: it is accusative by an omitted verb, which is the governing element of "qilan," i.e., "say: be at peace, peace." It was said: "salaman" is a substitute for "qilan." It was said: it is an attribute of "qilan" by the verbal noun, as if it were said: except a speech free from these defects.

﴿Among lote trees without thorns﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 28]: in Paradise is a tree of its own kind, having fruit like the jars of Hajar, good in taste and fragrance.
﴿Makhdud﴾: free of thorns. Mujahid said: makhdud is the one laden so heavily that its branches bend from the abundance of its fruit, from khadada al-ghusn when he bent it.
The majority read ﴿and banana trees﴾ with a ḥā'; 'Ali, Ja'far ibn Muhammad and 'Abdullah read it with an 'ayn, which he recited from the pulpit. 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' and Mujahid said: ṭalḥ is the banana. al-Hasan said: it is not the banana, but a tree whose shade is cool and moist. It was said: the tree of Umm Ghaylan, which has abundant, fragrant blossom. al-Suddi said: a tree resembling the ṭalḥ of this world, but its fruit is sweeter than honey. Manḍud: that which is arranged from its base to its top, so that no trunk appears.
﴿And extended shade﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 30]: that does not contract, but spreads out and is not abrogated by anything. Mujahid said: this shade is from its lote trees and its ṭalḥ trees.
﴿And water poured out﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 31]: Sufyan and others said: flowing without ditches. It was said: running freely, requiring no labor with a water-wheel or a bucket.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 56, verse 8–40 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Neither cut off﴾: that is, it is perpetual, never cut off at certain times as the fruit of this world is. ﴿Nor forbidden﴾: that is, one is not prevented from partaking of it in any way, and it is not forbidden to them as those in this world are.

It was also read as "wa-fakihatun kathirah" with both words in the nominative (marfu'an), meaning "and there is abundant fruit" [i.e., there is fruit there]. And "wa-furush" is the plural of firash. The majority (al-Jumhur) read it with a dammah on the ra' (furush); Abu Haywah read it with a sukun, marfu'ah, meaning they were arranged until they were raised up, or they were raised upon the beds. The apparent meaning is that the firash is that which is spread out for sitting upon and sleeping on.

Abu 'Ubaydah and others said: the intended meaning of "furush" is the women, because a woman is referred to by the firash, and [God] raised them in value and station. The pronoun in ﴿anshanahunna﴾ refers, in the view of Abu 'Ubaydah, to the furush, since they are the women in his view; and [according to what is indicated by the furush] if what is meant by the furush is the apparent meaning of what they indicate of the garments that are spread out and reclined upon. That is, We began their creation as a new beginning, without birth. The apparent meaning of al-insha' (the bringing into being) is the origination that was not preceded by creation, and this would be specific to the hur (the maidens of paradise) who are not of the offspring of Adam. It is possible that it means the re-creation (insha' al-i'adah), in which case it would apply to the daughters of Adam.

﴿So We made them virgins, 'uruban﴾: al-'Urub. Ibn 'Abbas said: al-'Urub are those who are loving toward their husbands; this was also said by al-Hasan. Ibn 'Abbas also described them as al-'awashiq (the ardent lovers), and from this is the verse of Labid:

"And among the curtains are 'urub, not lewd, / fragrant of hips, whose sight is veiled beyond them."

Ibn Zayd said: al-'Urub are those who beautify speech.

Hamzah and a group including Shuja', 'Abbas, and al-Asma'i (from Abu 'Amr), and a group including Kharijah, Kardam and Abu Khulayd (from Nafi'), and a group including Abu Bakr, Hammad and Aban (from 'Asim), read it with a sukun on the ra' (ʿurban), which is the dialect of Tamim; the rest of the seven read it with a dammah. (Atraban) [means] of the same form and stature. Whoever went to the view that the pronoun in ﴿anshanahunna﴾ refers to the maidens of paradise mentioned before was far off the mark, because that is a story already concluded, namely the story of the foremost (al-sabiqun), and this is the story of the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin). The lam in (li-ashab) is connected to anshanahunna.

﴿A company of the earlier generations﴾: that is, of the past nations, ﴿and a company of the later generations﴾: that is, of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). There is no contradiction between His saying ﴿and a company of the later generations﴾ and His saying earlier ﴿and few of the later generations﴾, because His saying ﴿of the later generations﴾ refers to the foremost, and His saying ﴿and a company of the later generations﴾ refers to the companions of the right.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 56, verse 8–40 (part 1 of 2):

﴿When the earth is shaken with a violent shaking﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 4]. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was convulsed and set in motion by a pull. He also said, together with 'Ikrimah and Mujahid, that (bussat) means: it was crumbled to dust. It was also said: it was set moving. Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﴿rujjat﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 4] and (bassat) in the active voice. (﴿Idha rujjat﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 4]) is a substitute for ﴿Idha waqa'at﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 1]. In my view the answer of the conditional is pronounced explicitly, namely His saying ﴿then the companions of the right hand﴾, and the meaning is: when such and such occurs, then the companions of the right hand — how happy they are, and how great is the reward they will receive. That is, their happiness and the greatness of their rank with Allah will become manifest at that severe and difficult time for the world. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that it be in the accusative governed by "lowering and raising" (khafidhah rafi'ah), i.e., it lowers and raises at the time the earth is shaken and the mountains are crumbled, because at that time what is high is lowered and what is low is raised. End of quotation. It is not permissible for it to be governed by both of them together; rather by one of them, since two governing agents cannot act upon one effect. Ibn Jinni and Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: ﴿Idha rujjat﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 4] is in the place of nominative, as a predicate of the subject which is ﴿Idha waqa'at﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 1]; neither of them is conditional, rather (idha) is used in the sense of "time," and what follows idha are three states. The meaning: the time of the occurrence of the Event, when it truly occurs, lowering some people and raising others, is the time the earth is shaken. Likewise Ibn Malik claimed that idha may be a subject, and he took this as evidence. We have mentioned in our commentary on al-Tashil what keeps idha within its signification of the conditional, and the explanation of (al-habaa') has already been given in surah al-Furqan.
﴿Munbaththan﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 6]: scattered. Written with two dots (munbattan) in place of the three-dotted thā', the reading of the majority, i.e., cut off.
(And you were): an address to the world, ﴿three kinds﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 7]: three categories. These are the ranks of people on the Day of Resurrection.
﴿Then the companions of the right hand﴾: al-Hasan and al-Rabi' said: they are the blessed ones with respect to themselves. It was said: those who are given their records in their right hands. It was said: the people of lofty rank, as you say: "he is to me on the right" (bil-yamin). It was said: those who are taken to the right side, or the right side of Adam mentioned in the event of the Night Journey, in the black figures.
﴿And the companions of the left hand﴾: they are those who oppose the companions of the right hand in these sayings. Here "companions" (ashab) is the subject, "what" (ma) is a second subject interrogative in the sense of magnification, and "companions of the right hand" is the predicate of "what," and what follows it is the predicate of "companions." The sentence is linked to the subject by repeating the subject with its wording, which most often occurs in contexts of awe and magnification. "What" expresses wonder at the state of the two groups in happiness and wretchedness; the meaning is: what a state they are in.
﴿And the foremost, the foremost﴾: they permitted that it be a subject and predicate, like the saying "you are you" and the verse "I am Abu al-Najm" and "my poetry is my poetry," meaning: those who excelled in precedence, i.e., in acts of obedience, and excelled in them, and whose state is known. And that "the foremost" be an emphatic repetition, with the predicate following that. And that "the foremost" be the subject, with the predicate following it, and you stop at his saying "and the foremost"; and that the object of the first precedence differ from the second precedence: the foremost to faith are the foremost to Paradise. On this view they permitted that "the foremost" be the predicate of his saying "and the foremost," and that it be an attribute with the predicate following. The first view: Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Sibawayh's view is that "the foremost" is the predicate of the subject, meaning the predicate of "and the foremost," and this is like saying "the people, the people," or "you, you," and this is for the sake of magnifying and exalting the matter. End of quotation. This view is favored by the fact that He mentioned the companions of the right hand, marveling at their happiness, and the companions of the left hand, marveling at their wretchedness, so it fits that He mention the foremost, affirming their state in a magnifying manner, by informing that they are at the utmost in greatness and happiness. "The foremost" is general in precedence to acts of obedience and to abandoning sins. 'Uthman ibn Abi Sawdah said: the foremost to the mosques. Ibn Sirin said: they are those who prayed toward both qiblahs. Ka'b said: they are the people of the Qur'an. And in a hadith: "He was asked about the foremost, and he said: they are those who, when given the truth, accept it, and when asked for it, they give it, and they judge people by the judgment they apply to themselves."
(Ulā'ika): a reference to the foremost, the drawn-near, whose ranks are high and whose degrees in Paradise are close to the Throne. The majority read ﴿fi jannat﴾ in the plural; Talhah read "fi jannah" in the singular. He divided the foremost, the drawn-near, into ﴿a multitude from the earlier peoples and a few from the later peoples﴾. Al-Hasan said: the foremost are from the nations, and the foremost are from this community. 'A'ishah said: the two groups exist in every prophet's nation: at its beginning is a multitude, and at its end a few. It was said: they are the prophets, peace be upon them, who were at the beginning of the world, and at its end fewer. And in a hadith: "The two groups are in my community: the foremost at the beginning of the community is a multitude, and the foremost of its remainder until the Day of Resurrection is a few." And "a multitude" is in the nominative by supposing them (ارتفع ثلة على إضمارهم).
The majority read ﴿on thrones﴾ with a dammah on the rā'; Zayd ibn 'Ali and Abu al-Sammal read it with a fatha, a dialect of some Banu Tamim and Kalb, who pronounce the 'ayn of fu'ul, the plural of the doubled fa'il, with a fatha, as in sarir; this was mentioned in al-Saffat.
﴿Mawdunah﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 15]: Ibn 'Abbas said: interwoven with gold. 'Ikrimah said: interlaced with pearls and rubies.
﴿Reclining upon them﴾: that is, upon the thrones; "reclining" is a circumstantial state of the pronoun hidden in ﴿on thrones﴾; (facing one another): each looks at the other. They are described with good companionship, refinement of character, and the purity of their inner selves from rancor, as brothers.
﴿There will circulate among them young boys made eternal﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 17]: they are described as eternal, though everyone in Paradise is eternal, to show that they remain forever in the age of youth, not aging nor changing from the form of youthful bloom. Mujahid said: they do not die. Al-Farra' said: adorned with earrings of the kind called khaladat, which are types of earrings.
﴿And a cup from a flowing spring﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 18]: he said: of wine flowing, running, and streaming.
﴿They will not be stupefied by it﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 19]: most said: the headache that comes from the wine of this world does not reach their heads. I read to our teacher, the eminent scholar Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah have mercy on him, the words of 'Alqamah describing wine:
"It cures headache, and its pourer does not harm you, nor does a dizziness enter the head."
He said: this is a description of the people of Paradise. It was also said: they are not separated from it, meaning: their pleasure is not cut off from them by any cause, as the wine of this world separates its people in various ways of separation, as in the saying: "so the cloud split (tasadda'a) from the city," i.e., it dispersed. Mujahid read "la yassaddda'una" with a fatha on the yā' and a shadda on the ṣād, its original form being yatasaddda'una, the tā' assimilated into the ṣād: i.e., they will not disperse, like His saying: ﴿on that day they will be split apart﴾ [al-Rum: 43]. The majority read with a ḍammah on the yā' and a light ṣād. The majority read "and fruit" and "and meat" in the genitive; Zayd ibn 'Ali read them in the nominative, meaning: and for them. The majority read ﴿nor will they be drained﴾ in the passive. Mujahid, Qatadah, Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: their minds do not depart through intoxication. Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with a fatha on the yā' and a kasra on the zāy, from nazafa the well: he drained its water; the meaning: their wine will not run out. Ibn Abi Ishaq also, 'Abdullah, al-Sulami, al-Jahdari, al-A'mash, Talhah and 'Isa read it with a ḍammah on the yā' and a kasra on the zāy: i.e., their drink will not be exhausted. ﴿From what they choose﴾: they take its best and finest. ﴿From what they desire﴾: i.e., what they wish for.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that it be in the accusative governed by "lowering and raising" (khafidhah rafi'ah), i.e., it lowers and raises at the time the earth is shaken and the mountains are crumbled, because at that time what is high is lowered and what is low is raised. Ibn Jinni and Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: ﴿Idha rujjat﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 4] is in the place of nominative, as a predicate of the subject which is ﴿Idha waqa'at﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 1]; neither of them is conditional, rather (idha) is used in the sense of "time," and what follows idha are three states. The meaning: the time of the occurrence of the Event, when it truly occurs, lowering some people and raising others, is the time the earth is shaken. Likewise Ibn Malik claimed that idha may be a subject, and he took this as evidence. We have mentioned in our commentary on al-Tashil what keeps idha within its signification of the conditional, and the explanation of (al-habaa') has already been given in surah al-Furqan.
﴿Munbaththan﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 6]: scattered. Written with two dots (munbattan) in place of the three-dotted thā', the reading of the majority, i.e., cut off.
(And you were): an address to the world, ﴿three kinds﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 7]: three categories. These are the ranks of people on the Day of Resurrection.
﴿Then the companions of the right hand﴾: al-Hasan and al-Rabi' said: they are the blessed ones with respect to themselves. It was said: those who are given their records in their right hands. It was said: the people of lofty rank, as you say: "he is to me on the right" (bil-yamin). It was said: those who are taken to the right side, or the right side of Adam mentioned in the event of the Night Journey, in the black figures.
﴿And the companions of the left hand﴾: they are those who oppose the companions of the right hand in these sayings. Here "companions" (ashab) is the subject, "what" (ma) is a second subject interrogative in the sense of magnification, and "companions of the right hand" is the predicate of "what," and what follows it is the predicate of "companions." The sentence is linked to the subject by repeating the subject with its wording, which most often occurs in contexts of awe and magnification. "What" expresses wonder at the state of the two groups in happiness and wretchedness; the meaning is: what a state they are in.
﴿And the foremost, the foremost﴾: they permitted that it be a subject and predicate, like the saying "you are you" and the verse "I am Abu al-Najm" and "my poetry is my poetry," meaning: those who excelled in precedence, i.e., in acts of obedience, and excelled in them, and whose state is known. And that "the foremost" be an emphatic repetition, with the predicate following that. And that "the foremost" be the subject, with the predicate following it, and you stop at his saying "and the foremost"; and that the object of the first precedence differ from the second precedence: the foremost to faith are the foremost to Paradise. On this view they permitted that "the foremost" be the predicate of his saying "and the foremost," and that it be an attribute with the predicate following. The first view: Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Sibawayh's view is that "the foremost" is the predicate of the subject, meaning the predicate of "and the foremost," and this is like saying "the people, the people," or "you, you," and this is for the sake of magnifying and exalting the matter. End of quotation. This view is favored by the fact that He mentioned the companions of the right hand, marveling at their happiness, and the companions of the left hand, marveling at their wretchedness, so it fits that He mention the foremost, affirming their state in a magnifying manner, by informing that they are at the utmost in greatness and happiness. "The foremost" is general in precedence to acts of obedience and to abandoning sins. 'Uthman ibn Abi Sawdah said: the foremost to the mosques. Ibn Sirin said: they are those who prayed toward both qiblahs. Ka'b said: they are the people of the Qur'an. And in a hadith: "He was asked about the foremost, and he said: they are those who, when given the truth, accept it, and when asked for it, they give it, and they judge people by the judgment they apply to themselves."
(Ulā'ika): a reference to the foremost, the drawn-near, whose ranks are high and whose degrees in Paradise are close to the Throne. The majority read ﴿fi jannat﴾ in the plural; Talhah read "fi jannah" in the singular. He divided the foremost, the drawn-near, into ﴿a multitude from the earlier peoples and a few from the later peoples﴾. Al-Hasan said: the foremost are from the nations, and the foremost are from this community. 'A'ishah said: the two groups exist in every prophet's nation: at its beginning is a multitude, and at its end a few. It was said: they are the prophets, peace be upon them, who were at the beginning of the world, and at its end fewer. And in a hadith: "The two groups are in my community: the foremost at the beginning of the community is a multitude, and the foremost of its remainder until the Day of Resurrection is a few." And "a multitude" is in the nominative by supposing them (ارتفع ثلة على إضمارهم).
The majority read ﴿on thrones﴾ with a dammah on the rā'; Zayd ibn 'Ali and Abu al-Sammal read it with a fatha, a dialect of some Banu Tamim and Kalb, who pronounce the 'ayn of fu'ul, the plural of the doubled fa'il, with a fatha, as in sarir; this was mentioned in al-Saffat.
﴿Mawdunah﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 15]: Ibn 'Abbas said: interwoven with gold. 'Ikrimah said: interlaced with pearls and rubies.
﴿Reclining upon them﴾: that is, upon the thrones; "reclining" is a circumstantial state of the pronoun hidden in ﴿on thrones﴾; (facing one another): each looks at the other. They are described with good companionship, refinement of character, and the purity of their inner selves from rancor, as brothers.
﴿There will circulate among them young boys made eternal﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 17]: they are described as eternal, though everyone in Paradise is eternal, to show that they remain forever in the age of youth, not aging nor changing from the form of youthful bloom. Mujahid said: they do not die. Al-Farra' said: adorned with earrings of the kind called khaladat, which are types of earrings.
﴿And a cup from a flowing spring﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 18]: he said: of wine flowing, running, and streaming.
﴿They will not be stupefied by it﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 19]: most said: the headache that comes from the wine of this world does not reach their heads. I read to our teacher, the eminent scholar Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah have mercy on him, the words of 'Alqamah describing wine:
"It cures headache, and its pourer does not harm you, nor does a dizziness enter the head."
He said: this is a description of the people of Paradise. It was also said: they are not separated from it, meaning: their pleasure is not cut off from them by any cause, as the wine of this world separates its people in various ways of separation, as in the saying: "so the cloud split (tasadda'a) from the city," i.e., it dispersed. Mujahid read "la yassaddda'una" with a fatha on the yā' and a shadda on the ṣād, its original form being yatasaddda'una, the tā' assimilated into the ṣād: i.e., they will not disperse, like His saying: ﴿on that day they will be split apart﴾ [al-Rum: 43]. The majority read with a ḍammah on the yā' and a light ṣād. The majority read "and fruit" and "and meat" in the genitive; Zayd ibn 'Ali read them in the nominative, meaning: and for them. The majority read ﴿nor will they be drained﴾ in the passive. Mujahid, Qatadah, Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: their minds do not depart through intoxication. Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with a fatha on the yā' and a kasra on the zāy, from nazafa the well: he drained its water; the meaning: their wine will not run out. Ibn Abi Ishaq also, 'Abdullah, al-Sulami, al-Jahdari, al-A'mash, Talhah and 'Isa read it with a ḍammah on the yā' and a kasra on the zāy: i.e., their drink will not be exhausted. ﴿From what they choose﴾: they take its best and finest. ﴿From what they desire﴾: i.e., what they wish for.
The majority read ﴿and houris with wide, lovely eyes﴾ in the nominative; 'Ali explained it as being conjoined to "young boys," or to the hidden pronoun in "reclining," or to an omitted subject with its predicate, the estimate being: for them is all this, ﴿and houris with wide, lovely eyes﴾, or with only the predicate omitted: i.e., and for them are houris, or in them are houris. Al-Sulami, al-Hasan, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, al-A'mash, Talhah, al-Mufaddal, Aban, 'Isma and al-Kisa'i read them in the genitive; al-Nakha'i read "wa-hiyar 'in" with the wāw changed to yā' and both in the genitive; the genitive is conjoined to the preceding genitive, meaning: young boys go around them with such and such and with houris with wide, lovely eyes. It was also said: it means: they are blessed with all this and with houris with wide, lovely eyes. Al-Zamakhshari said: conjoined to "gardens of bliss," as if he said: they are in gardens, fruit, meat and houris. End of quotation. This has remoteness and breaks up a speech whose parts are linked to one another; it is a non-Arabic understanding. Ubayy and 'Abdullah read "wa-hūran 'īnan" in the accusative, and they said: on the meaning of "and they are given all this and houris with wide, lovely eyes." Qatadah read "wa-ḥūru 'īnin" in the nominative, annexed to "'īn"; Ibn Miqsam read it in the accusative, annexed to "'īn"; 'Ikrimah read "wa-ḥawrā' 'ayna'" in the singular as a noun of genus, and with a fatha on the hamza in both; it may be genitive, conjoined to the preceding genitive, or accusative, like the reading of Ubayy and 'Abdullah, "wa-ḥūran 'īnan."

He described the pearl as "hidden" (maknun), because it is purest and furthest from change. In a hadith: "Their purity is like the purity of the pearl that no hand has touched." Allah said: ﴿as if they were hidden eggs﴾ [al-Saffat: 49]. A poet, describing a woman as chaste and unexposed to wear, likened her to a hidden pearl in its shell, saying:
"She stood displaying herself between the two curtains of a veil, like the sun on the day of its rising amid the stars.
Or a pearl of the Sadaf sea, whose diver is delighted; when he sees it, he rejoices and prostrates."

﴿A reward for what they used to do﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 24]: it is narrated that the dwellings and the divisions in Paradise are according to the measure of deeds, but entry into Paradise itself is by the mercy and grace of Allah, not by the deed of any doer; and in it is the clear, sound text: "No one will enter Paradise by his deeds." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His grace and mercy."

(Laghwan): idle talk and its vulgarity; ﴿nor sinful speech﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 25]: anything that makes anyone sinful. The apparent view is that ﴿except the word "Peace, peace"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 26] is a disjunctive exception, because it does not fall under idle talk or sin; the view of those who say it is a connected exception is remote. As for "salaman" (peace), al-Zajjaj said: it is a verbal noun whose accusative is governed by "qilan" (speech), i.e., one says to another "salaman salaman." It was said: it is accusative by an omitted verb, which is the governing element of "qilan," i.e., "say: be at peace, peace." It was said: "salaman" is a substitute for "qilan." It was said: it is an attribute of "qilan" by the verbal noun, as if it were said: except a speech free from these defects.

﴿Among lote trees without thorns﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 28]: in Paradise is a tree of its own kind, having fruit like the jars of Hajar, good in taste and fragrance.
﴿Makhdud﴾: free of thorns. Mujahid said: makhdud is the one laden so heavily that its branches bend from the abundance of its fruit, from khadada al-ghusn when he bent it.
The majority read ﴿and banana trees﴾ with a ḥā'; 'Ali, Ja'far ibn Muhammad and 'Abdullah read it with an 'ayn, which he recited from the pulpit. 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' and Mujahid said: ṭalḥ is the banana. al-Hasan said: it is not the banana, but a tree whose shade is cool and moist. It was said: the tree of Umm Ghaylan, which has abundant, fragrant blossom. al-Suddi said: a tree resembling the ṭalḥ of this world, but its fruit is sweeter than honey. Manḍud: that which is arranged from its base to its top, so that no trunk appears.
﴿And extended shade﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 30]: that does not contract, but spreads out and is not abrogated by anything. Mujahid said: this shade is from its lote trees and its ṭalḥ trees.
﴿And water poured out﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 31]: Sufyan and others said: flowing without ditches. It was said: running freely, requiring no labor with a water-wheel or a bucket.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 56, verse 8–40 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Neither cut off﴾: that is, it is perpetual, never cut off at certain times as the fruit of this world is. ﴿Nor forbidden﴾: that is, one is not prevented from partaking of it in any way, and it is not forbidden to them as those in this world are.

It was also read as "wa-fakihatun kathirah" with both words in the nominative (marfu'an), meaning "and there is abundant fruit" [i.e., there is fruit there]. And "wa-furush" is the plural of firash. The majority (al-Jumhur) read it with a dammah on the ra' (furush); Abu Haywah read it with a sukun, marfu'ah, meaning they were arranged until they were raised up, or they were raised upon the beds. The apparent meaning is that the firash is that which is spread out for sitting upon and sleeping on.

Abu 'Ubaydah and others said: the intended meaning of "furush" is the women, because a woman is referred to by the firash, and [God] raised them in value and station. The pronoun in ﴿anshanahunna﴾ refers, in the view of Abu 'Ubaydah, to the furush, since they are the women in his view; and [according to what is indicated by the furush] if what is meant by the furush is the apparent meaning of what they indicate of the garments that are spread out and reclined upon. That is, We began their creation as a new beginning, without birth. The apparent meaning of al-insha' (the bringing into being) is the origination that was not preceded by creation, and this would be specific to the hur (the maidens of paradise) who are not of the offspring of Adam. It is possible that it means the re-creation (insha' al-i'adah), in which case it would apply to the daughters of Adam.

﴿So We made them virgins, 'uruban﴾: al-'Urub. Ibn 'Abbas said: al-'Urub are those who are loving toward their husbands; this was also said by al-Hasan. Ibn 'Abbas also described them as al-'awashiq (the ardent lovers), and from this is the verse of Labid:

"And among the curtains are 'urub, not lewd, / fragrant of hips, whose sight is veiled beyond them."

Ibn Zayd said: al-'Urub are those who beautify speech.

Hamzah and a group including Shuja', 'Abbas, and al-Asma'i (from Abu 'Amr), and a group including Kharijah, Kardam and Abu Khulayd (from Nafi'), and a group including Abu Bakr, Hammad and Aban (from 'Asim), read it with a sukun on the ra' (ʿurban), which is the dialect of Tamim; the rest of the seven read it with a dammah. (Atraban) [means] of the same form and stature. Whoever went to the view that the pronoun in ﴿anshanahunna﴾ refers to the maidens of paradise mentioned before was far off the mark, because that is a story already concluded, namely the story of the foremost (al-sabiqun), and this is the story of the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin). The lam in (li-ashab) is connected to anshanahunna.

﴿A company of the earlier generations﴾: that is, of the past nations, ﴿and a company of the later generations﴾: that is, of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). There is no contradiction between His saying ﴿and a company of the later generations﴾ and His saying earlier ﴿and few of the later generations﴾, because His saying ﴿of the later generations﴾ refers to the foremost, and His saying ﴿and a company of the later generations﴾ refers to the companions of the right.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 56, verse 8–40 (part 1 of 2):

﴿When the earth is shaken with a violent shaking﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 4]. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was convulsed and set in motion by a pull. He also said, together with 'Ikrimah and Mujahid, that (bussat) means: it was crumbled to dust. It was also said: it was set moving. Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﴿rujjat﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 4] and (bassat) in the active voice. (﴿Idha rujjat﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 4]) is a substitute for ﴿Idha waqa'at﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 1]. In my view the answer of the conditional is pronounced explicitly, namely His saying ﴿then the companions of the right hand﴾, and the meaning is: when such and such occurs, then the companions of the right hand — how happy they are, and how great is the reward they will receive. That is, their happiness and the greatness of their rank with Allah will become manifest at that severe and difficult time for the world. And that "the foremost" be the subject, with the predicate following it, and you stop at his saying "and the foremost"; and that the object of the first precedence differ from the second precedence: the foremost to faith are the foremost to Paradise. On this view they permitted that "the foremost" be the predicate of his saying "and the foremost," and that it be an attribute with the predicate following. End of quotation. This view is favored by the fact that He mentioned the companions of the right hand, marveling at their happiness, and the companions of the left hand, marveling at their wretchedness, so it fits that He mention the foremost, affirming their state in a magnifying manner, by informing that they are at the utmost in greatness and happiness. He described the pearl as "hidden" (maknun), because it is purest and furthest from change. In a hadith: "Their purity is like the purity of the pearl that no hand has touched." Allah said: ﴿as if they were hidden eggs﴾ [al-Saffat: 49]. A poet, describing a woman as chaste and unexposed to wear, likened her to a hidden pearl in its shell, saying:
"She stood displaying herself between the two curtains of a veil, like the sun on the day of its rising amid the stars.
Or a pearl of the Sadaf sea, whose diver is delighted; when he sees it, he rejoices and prostrates."

﴿A reward for what they used to do﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 24]: it is narrated that the dwellings and the divisions in Paradise are according to the measure of deeds, but entry into Paradise itself is by the mercy and grace of Allah, not by the deed of any doer; and in it is the clear, sound text: "No one will enter Paradise by his deeds." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His grace and mercy."

(Laghwan): idle talk and its vulgarity; ﴿nor sinful speech﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 25]: anything that makes anyone sinful. The apparent view is that ﴿except the word "Peace, peace"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 26] is a disjunctive exception, because it does not fall under idle talk or sin; the view of those who say it is a connected exception is remote. As for "salaman" (peace), al-Zajjaj said: it is a verbal noun whose accusative is governed by "qilan" (speech), i.e., one says to another "salaman salaman." It was said: it is accusative by an omitted verb, which is the governing element of "qilan," i.e., "say: be at peace, peace." It was said: "salaman" is a substitute for "qilan." It was said: it is an attribute of "qilan" by the verbal noun, as if it were said: except a speech free from these defects.

﴿Among lote trees without thorns﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 28]: in Paradise is a tree of its own kind, having fruit like the jars of Hajar, good in taste and fragrance.
﴿Makhdud﴾: free of thorns. Mujahid said: makhdud is the one laden so heavily that its branches bend from the abundance of its fruit, from khadada al-ghusn when he bent it.
The majority read ﴿and banana trees﴾ with a ḥā'; 'Ali, Ja'far ibn Muhammad and 'Abdullah read it with an 'ayn, which he recited from the pulpit. 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' and Mujahid said: ṭalḥ is the banana. al-Hasan said: it is not the banana, but a tree whose shade is cool and moist. It was said: the tree of Umm Ghaylan, which has abundant, fragrant blossom. al-Suddi said: a tree resembling the ṭalḥ of this world, but its fruit is sweeter than honey. Manḍud: that which is arranged from its base to its top, so that no trunk appears.
﴿And extended shade﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 30]: that does not contract, but spreads out and is not abrogated by anything. Mujahid said: this shade is from its lote trees and its ṭalḥ trees.
﴿And water poured out﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 31]: Sufyan and others said: flowing without ditches. It was said: running freely, requiring no labor with a water-wheel or a bucket.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 56, verse 8–40 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Neither cut off﴾: that is, it is perpetual, never cut off at certain times as the fruit of this world is. ﴿Nor forbidden﴾: that is, one is not prevented from partaking of it in any way, and it is not forbidden to them as those in this world are.

It was also read as "wa-fakihatun kathirah" with both words in the nominative (marfu'an), meaning "and there is abundant fruit" [i.e., there is fruit there]. And "wa-furush" is the plural of firash. The majority (al-Jumhur) read it with a dammah on the ra' (furush); Abu Haywah read it with a sukun, marfu'ah, meaning they were arranged until they were raised up, or they were raised upon the beds. The apparent meaning is that the firash is that which is spread out for sitting upon and sleeping on.

Abu 'Ubaydah and others said: the intended meaning of "furush" is the women, because a woman is referred to by the firash, and [God] raised them in value and station. The pronoun in ﴿anshanahunna﴾ refers, in the view of Abu 'Ubaydah, to the furush, since they are the women in his view; and [according to what is indicated by the furush] if what is meant by the furush is the apparent meaning of what they indicate of the garments that are spread out and reclined upon. That is, We began their creation as a new beginning, without birth. The apparent meaning of al-insha' (the bringing into being) is the origination that was not preceded by creation, and this would be specific to the hur (the maidens of paradise) who are not of the offspring of Adam. It is possible that it means the re-creation (insha' al-i'adah), in which case it would apply to the daughters of Adam.

﴿So We made them virgins, 'uruban﴾: al-'Urub. Ibn 'Abbas said: al-'Urub are those who are loving toward their husbands; this was also said by al-Hasan. Ibn 'Abbas also described them as al-'awashiq (the ardent lovers), and from this is the verse of Labid:

"And among the curtains are 'urub, not lewd, / fragrant of hips, whose sight is veiled beyond them."

Ibn Zayd said: al-'Urub are those who beautify speech.

Hamzah and a group including Shuja', 'Abbas, and al-Asma'i (from Abu 'Amr), and a group including Kharijah, Kardam and Abu Khulayd (from Nafi'), and a group including Abu Bakr, Hammad and Aban (from 'Asim), read it with a sukun on the ra' (ʿurban), which is the dialect of Tamim; the rest of the seven read it with a dammah. (Atraban) [means] of the same form and stature. Whoever went to the view that the pronoun in ﴿anshanahunna﴾ refers to the maidens of paradise mentioned before was far off the mark, because that is a story already concluded, namely the story of the foremost (al-sabiqun), and this is the story of the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin). The lam in (li-ashab) is connected to anshanahunna.

﴿A company of the earlier generations﴾: that is, of the past nations, ﴿and a company of the later generations﴾: that is, of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). There is no contradiction between His saying ﴿and a company of the later generations﴾ and His saying earlier ﴿and few of the later generations﴾, because His saying ﴿of the later generations﴾ refers to the foremost, and His saying ﴿and a company of the later generations﴾ refers to the companions of the right.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 56, verse 8–40 (part 1 of 2):

﴿When the earth is shaken with a violent shaking﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 4]. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was convulsed and set in motion by a pull. He also said, together with 'Ikrimah and Mujahid, that (bussat) means: it was crumbled to dust. It was also said: it was set moving. Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﴿rujjat﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 4] and (bassat) in the active voice. (﴿Idha rujjat﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 4]) is a substitute for ﴿Idha waqa'at﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 1]. In my view the answer of the conditional is pronounced explicitly, namely His saying ﴿then the companions of the right hand﴾, and the meaning is: when such and such occurs, then the companions of the right hand — how happy they are, and how great is the reward they will receive. That is, their happiness and the greatness of their rank with Allah will become manifest at that severe and difficult time for the world. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that it be in the accusative governed by "lowering and raising" (khafidhah rafi'ah), i.e., it lowers and raises at the time the earth is shaken and the mountains are crumbled, because at that time what is high is lowered and what is low is raised. End of quotation. It is not permissible for it to be governed by both of them together; rather by one of them, since two governing agents cannot act upon one effect. Ibn Jinni and Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: ﴿Idha rujjat﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 4] is in the place of nominative, as a predicate of the subject which is ﴿Idha waqa'at﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 1]; neither of them is conditional, rather (idha) is used in the sense of "time," and what follows idha are three states. The meaning: the time of the occurrence of the Event, when it truly occurs, lowering some people and raising others, is the time the earth is shaken. Likewise Ibn Malik claimed that idha may be a subject, and he took this as evidence. We have mentioned in our commentary on al-Tashil what keeps idha within its signification of the conditional, and the explanation of (al-habaa') has already been given in surah al-Furqan.
﴿Munbaththan﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 6]: scattered. Written with two dots (munbattan) in place of the three-dotted thā', the reading of the majority, i.e., cut off.
(And you were): an address to the world, ﴿three kinds﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 7]: three categories. These are the ranks of people on the Day of Resurrection.
﴿Then the companions of the right hand﴾: al-Hasan and al-Rabi' said: they are the blessed ones with respect to themselves. It was said: those who are given their records in their right hands. It was said: the people of lofty rank, as you say: "he is to me on the right" (bil-yamin). It was said: those who are taken to the right side, or the right side of Adam mentioned in the event of the Night Journey, in the black figures.
﴿And the companions of the left hand﴾: they are those who oppose the companions of the right hand in these sayings. Here "companions" (ashab) is the subject, "what" (ma) is a second subject interrogative in the sense of magnification, and "companions of the right hand" is the predicate of "what," and what follows it is the predicate of "companions." The sentence is linked to the subject by repeating the subject with its wording, which most often occurs in contexts of awe and magnification. "What" expresses wonder at the state of the two groups in happiness and wretchedness; the meaning is: what a state they are in.
﴿And the foremost, the foremost﴾: they permitted that it be a subject and predicate, like the saying "you are you" and the verse "I am Abu al-Najm" and "my poetry is my poetry," meaning: those who excelled in precedence, i.e., in acts of obedience, and excelled in them, and whose state is known. And that "the foremost" be an emphatic repetition, with the predicate following that. And that "the foremost" be the subject, with the predicate following it, and you stop at his saying "and the foremost"; and that the object of the first precedence differ from the second precedence: the foremost to faith are the foremost to Paradise. On this view they permitted that "the foremost" be the predicate of his saying "and the foremost," and that it be an attribute with the predicate following. The first view: Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Sibawayh's view is that "the foremost" is the predicate of the subject, meaning the predicate of "and the foremost," and this is like saying "the people, the people," or "you, you," and this is for the sake of magnifying and exalting the matter. End of quotation. This view is favored by the fact that He mentioned the companions of the right hand, marveling at their happiness, and the companions of the left hand, marveling at their wretchedness, so it fits that He mention the foremost, affirming their state in a magnifying manner, by informing that they are at the utmost in greatness and happiness. "The foremost" is general in precedence to acts of obedience and to abandoning sins. 'Uthman ibn Abi Sawdah said: the foremost to the mosques. Ibn Sirin said: they are those who prayed toward both qiblahs. Ka'b said: they are the people of the Qur'an. And in a hadith: "He was asked about the foremost, and he said: they are those who, when given the truth, accept it, and when asked for it, they give it, and they judge people by the judgment they apply to themselves."
(Ulā'ika): a reference to the foremost, the drawn-near, whose ranks are high and whose degrees in Paradise are close to the Throne. The majority read ﴿fi jannat﴾ in the plural; Talhah read "fi jannah" in the singular. He divided the foremost, the drawn-near, into ﴿a multitude from the earlier peoples and a few from the later peoples﴾. Al-Hasan said: the foremost are from the nations, and the foremost are from this community. 'A'ishah said: the two groups exist in every prophet's nation: at its beginning is a multitude, and at its end a few. It was said: they are the prophets, peace be upon them, who were at the beginning of the world, and at its end fewer. And in a hadith: "The two groups are in my community: the foremost at the beginning of the community is a multitude, and the foremost of its remainder until the Day of Resurrection is a few." And "a multitude" is in the nominative by supposing them (ارتفع ثلة على إضمارهم).
The majority read ﴿on thrones﴾ with a dammah on the rā'; Zayd ibn 'Ali and Abu al-Sammal read it with a fatha, a dialect of some Banu Tamim and Kalb, who pronounce the 'ayn of fu'ul, the plural of the doubled fa'il, with a fatha, as in sarir; this was mentioned in al-Saffat.
﴿Mawdunah﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 15]: Ibn 'Abbas said: interwoven with gold. 'Ikrimah said: interlaced with pearls and rubies.
﴿Reclining upon them﴾: that is, upon the thrones; "reclining" is a circumstantial state of the pronoun hidden in ﴿on thrones﴾; (facing one another): each looks at the other. They are described with good companionship, refinement of character, and the purity of their inner selves from rancor, as brothers.
﴿There will circulate among them young boys made eternal﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 17]: they are described as eternal, though everyone in Paradise is eternal, to show that they remain forever in the age of youth, not aging nor changing from the form of youthful bloom. Mujahid said: they do not die. Al-Farra' said: adorned with earrings of the kind called khaladat, which are types of earrings.
﴿And a cup from a flowing spring﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 18]: he said: of wine flowing, running, and streaming.
﴿They will not be stupefied by it﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 19]: most said: the headache that comes from the wine of this world does not reach their heads. I read to our teacher, the eminent scholar Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah have mercy on him, the words of 'Alqamah describing wine:
"It cures headache, and its pourer does not harm you, nor does a dizziness enter the head."
He said: this is a description of the people of Paradise. It was also said: they are not separated from it, meaning: their pleasure is not cut off from them by any cause, as the wine of this world separates its people in various ways of separation, as in the saying: "so the cloud split (tasadda'a) from the city," i.e., it dispersed. Mujahid read "la yassaddda'una" with a fatha on the yā' and a shadda on the ṣād, its original form being yatasaddda'una, the tā' assimilated into the ṣād: i.e., they will not disperse, like His saying: ﴿on that day they will be split apart﴾ [al-Rum: 43]. The majority read with a ḍammah on the yā' and a light ṣād. The majority read "and fruit" and "and meat" in the genitive; Zayd ibn 'Ali read them in the nominative, meaning: and for them. The majority read ﴿nor will they be drained﴾ in the passive. Mujahid, Qatadah, Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: their minds do not depart through intoxication. Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with a fatha on the yā' and a kasra on the zāy, from nazafa the well: he drained its water; the meaning: their wine will not run out. Ibn Abi Ishaq also, 'Abdullah, al-Sulami, al-Jahdari, al-A'mash, Talhah and 'Isa read it with a ḍammah on the yā' and a kasra on the zāy: i.e., their drink will not be exhausted. ﴿From what they choose﴾: they take its best and finest. ﴿From what they desire﴾: i.e., what they wish for.
The majority read ﴿and houris with wide, lovely eyes﴾ in the nominative; 'Ali explained it as being conjoined to "young boys," or to the hidden pronoun in "reclining," or to an omitted subject with its predicate, the estimate being: for them is all this, ﴿and houris with wide, lovely eyes﴾, or with only the predicate omitted: i.e., and for them are houris, or in them are houris. Al-Sulami, al-Hasan, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, al-A'mash, Talhah, al-Mufaddal, Aban, 'Isma and al-Kisa'i read them in the genitive; al-Nakha'i read "wa-hiyar 'in" with the wāw changed to yā' and both in the genitive; the genitive is conjoined to the preceding genitive, meaning: young boys go around them with such and such and with houris with wide, lovely eyes. It was also said: it means: they are blessed with all this and with houris with wide, lovely eyes. Al-Zamakhshari said: conjoined to "gardens of bliss," as if he said: they are in gardens, fruit, meat and houris. End of quotation. This has remoteness and breaks up a speech whose parts are linked to one another; it is a non-Arabic understanding. Ubayy and 'Abdullah read "wa-hūran 'īnan" in the accusative, and they said: on the meaning of "and they are given all this and houris with wide, lovely eyes." Qatadah read "wa-ḥūru 'īnin" in the nominative, annexed to "'īn"; Ibn Miqsam read it in the accusative, annexed to "'īn"; 'Ikrimah read "wa-ḥawrā' 'ayna'" in the singular as a noun of genus, and with a fatha on the hamza in both; it may be genitive, conjoined to the preceding genitive, or accusative, like the reading of Ubayy and 'Abdullah, "wa-ḥūran 'īnan."
