With a fatha, it is like sahab and suhub; then it was lightened and what was done to the plural of ahyam was done to it, by changing its damma into a kasra so that the ya' is sound; or with a damma, it is pluralized on the pattern fi'l like qurad and qird, then the damma of the ra' was made sukun so it became fi'l, then what was done to bid' was done to it. Amnā al-rajul: the man emitted the seed; and manna: he expelled it from his urethra. Al-muzn: the clouds. The poet said:
"No cloud has poured its rain, nor has land grown its herbage."

Awrā al-nar min al-zinad: I struck the fire from the firestriker; the firestriker itself is kindled. The zinad is two stones or a stone and an iron, or of wood, especially soft wood like al-markh, al-'ifar and al-kalh. The Arabs strike with two sticks, rubbing one against the other, and they call the upper one al-zand and the lower one al-zanda, likening them to the wheel and the hole. Aqwā al-rajul: he entered the wasteland, al-qawā, which is the desert, like asḥar: he entered the open desert. Aqwā also means he stayed days without eating anything. Aqwat al-dar: the house became desolate. The poet said:
"O abode of Mayya at al-'Aliya and al-Sanad, it has become desolate and long ages have passed over it."

Idhdhahana: he was soft and gentle, and was lax in matters that are not borne by the one who is lax. The poet said:
"Resolve and strength are better than compromise, and than softness and weakness."

Al-hulqum: the passage of food. Al-rawh: rest. Al-rayhan has been discussed in Surat al-Rahman.

(p-209) When he mentioned the state of the foremost, and followed them with the companions of the right, he mentioned the state of the companions of the left, saying: ﴿And the companions of the left﴾. The i'rab of a similar sentence has preceded, and in this interrogation is the magnification of their calamity.

﴿In scorching wind﴾: in the most intense heat. ﴿And boiling water﴾: water of extreme heat.

﴿And a shade of black smoke﴾: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Abu Malik, Ibn Zayd and the majority said: smoke. Ibn 'Abbas also said: it is the enclosure of the Fire surrounding its people, rising from every side until it shades them. Ibn Kaysan said: al-yahmum is one of the names of Jahannam. Ibn Zayd also said, and Ibn Buraydah: it is a black mountain in the Fire, to which the people of the Fire flee for refuge, and they find it the most severe and bitter of things.

﴿Neither cool nor pleasant﴾: two attributes of the shade, negated. It is called a shade though it is not like shades, and its coolness and benefit to one who takes refuge in it are negated.

﴿Nor pleasant﴾: a completion of the negation of the attribute of praise in it, and an annihilation of what might be imagined in the shade of finding relief in it in the intensity of heat; or a negation of the honor of one who finds relief in it. It is attributed to it metaphorically, and what is meant is they, i.e., they seek shade in it while they are humiliated. It may also be understood as a bad gathering place, not a means of attaining honor. The first attribute mentioned is the essential one, which is the shade, and that it is "of black smoke," so it is a part of the yahmum. Then He negated of it the attribute that would make it a shade, which is being neither cool nor pleasant. It is also permissible that ﴿neither cool nor pleasant﴾ be an attribute of yahmum, and it would then follow that the shade is described by that. The majority read ﴿neither cool nor pleasant﴾ with the genitive on both; Ibn Abi 'Abla read them with the nominative: i.e., it is neither cool nor pleasant, in the manner of his saying:
"So I spend the night, neither sinful nor deprived."
i.e., I am neither sinful.

﴿Indeed, they were before that﴾: i.e., in the worldly life, ﴿affluent﴾: in this is a condemnation of affluence and luxury in this world, and affluence is a path to idleness and abandoning reflection on the outcome.

﴿And they used to persist﴾: i.e., they continued and were constant, ﴿in the great violation﴾. Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said: it is polytheism, and this is the apparent meaning. It was said: what is contained in His saying: ﴿And they swore by Allah their most emphatic oaths﴾ [al-Nahl: 38] and so on, of denial of resurrection. But the next phrase rules this out: ﴿And they used to say﴾, for it is conjoined to what precedes it, and conjunction requires difference; so the great violation is polytheism. Their saying: ﴿When we have died and become dust and bones, will we indeed be resurrected?﴾ ﴿And our forefathers, the earlier ones?﴾ has been discussed previously in al-Saffat. Al-Zamakhshari repeated here his misconception, saying: If you ask, how is the conjunction to the pronoun in (la-mab'uthun) good without emphasis by "nahnu"? I say: it is good because of the intervening element, which is the interrogative hamza, just as it is good in His saying: ﴿Neither we nor our forefathers have associated﴾ [al-An'am: 148], because of the intervening la, which emphasizes the negation. End. We have refuted him here and there, returning to the view of the majority that they do not posit between the interrogative hamza and the conjunctive particle a verb, as in: ﴿Have they not travelled﴾ [Yusuf: 109], (p-210) nor a noun, as in (awa-aba'una); rather the wa and the fa are for conjoining what follows them to what precedes them, and the hamza in the underlying structure is posterior to the conjunctive particle. But since the interrogative has the front position in speech, it was placed first.

When He mentioned their questioning about resurrection in the manner of disbelief and denial, He commanded His Prophet ﷺ to inform them of the resurrection of all the world, the first and the last of them, for reckoning, and of what the deniers of resurrection will reach of punishment. Al-miqat: that by which a thing is timed, i.e., limited, i.e., to what the world is timed by, a known day; and the idafa is in the sense of min, like "a ring of iron." (Then indeed you): an address to the disbelievers of Quraysh, ﴿O you who are astray﴾ from guidance, ﴿and deniers﴾ of resurrection. It is also an address to whoever follows their course in this.

﴿Will surely eat from a tree of zaqqum﴾: the first "min" is for the beginning of the limit or for partitive; the second, if min zaqqum is an apposition, then min admits both possibilities; if it is not an apposition, then it is for specifying the kind, i.e., from a tree which is zaqqum. The majority read min shajar; 'Abd Allah read min shajarah.

﴿And fill their bellies from it﴾: the pronoun in minha refers to shajar, since it is a collective noun that may be feminine or masculine; and on the reading of 'Abd Allah, it is clear.

﴿فَشارِبُونَ عَلَيْهِ﴾ [Qur'an 56:55]. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is mentioned according to the wording of "tree" (shajar), just as it is made feminine according to its meaning in "minhā" [Qur'an 56:52]. He said: As for the one who reads "min shajaratin min zaqqūm" [Qur'an 56:52], he has made both pronouns refer to the tree. The second pronoun is mentioned in accordance with the interpretation of zaqqūm, because it explains the tree, and it is in its meaning. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The pronoun in "'alayhi" refers to the food that is eaten, or to the eating. End of quote. He did not make it refer to "shajar" (tree). Nafi', 'Asim and Hamza read "shurb" (drinking) with a ḍammah on the shīn, and it is a maṣdar (verbal noun). It is said that it is an ism (noun) for what is drunk. Mujahid and Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi read it with a kasrah, and it has the meaning of "mashrūb" (what is drunk); it is an ism, not a maṣdar, like "ṭaḥn" (grinding) and "ra'y" (pasturing). Al-A'raj, Ibn al-Musayyab, Shu'ayb ibn al-Ḥabḥāb, Malik ibn Dinar, Ibn Jurayj and the rest of the Seven read it with a fatḥah, and it is a regular maṣdar. (The Seven: the seven canonical readers of the Qur'an.)

"Al-Hīm" (the thirsty camels): Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrima and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said it is the plural of "ahyam", which is the camel afflicted by al-hiyām (a disease of extreme thirst), and we have explained it in the Mufradāt (the lexicon of Qur'anic vocabulary). It is also said that it is the plural of "hay'ā'" (feminine). It is also said that it is the plural of "hā'im" and "hā'ima" (wandering), and the plural of the pattern fā'il on the pattern fi'l is irregular, like "bādhil" and "bidhl", and "ā'idh" and "i'dh". The "hā'im" also comes from al-hiyām. Do you not see that when a camel is afflicted by that, it wanders aimlessly and goes away? Ibn 'Abbas and Sufyan said: "al-Hīm" are the sands that are not quenched by water. The disagreement regarding its singular has already passed: is it "al-Hiyām" with a fatḥah on the hā', or with a ḍammah?

The meaning is: He will impose upon them, from hunger, what compels them to eat the zaqqūm, which is like molten metal (al-muhl). When they fill their bellies with it, He will impose upon them, from thirst, what compels them to drink the ḥamīm (boiling water), which cuts their intestines, so they drink it as thirsty camels drink. Al-Zamakhshari said this.

He also said: If you say: how is it correct to conjoin "shāribūn" to "shāribūn", when they refer to the same persons and are two identical attributes, so it would be conjunction of a thing with itself? I say: They are not identical, because their being drinkers of the ḥamīm in the state of extreme heat and cutting of the intestines is an astonishing matter, and their drinking it in such a way, as thirsty camels drink water, is also an astonishing matter. Thus they are two different attributes. End of quote.

The fā' (then) indicates sequence between the two drinkings: when they first became thirsty, they drank of the ḥamīm, thinking that it would quench their thirst, but the thirst increased because of the heat of the ḥamīm. So they drank after it a drinking by which they never attain satisfaction, and that is like the drinking of the thirsty camels. Thus these are two drinkings of ḥamīm, not one drinking; its attributes differ, so it is conjoined, and the intended point is the attribute. The object from which they drink in ﴿فَشارِبُونَ شُرْبَ الْهِيمِ﴾ is elided because the meaning is understood. Its estimated form is: "fa-shāribūna minhu shurba al-hīm" (so you will drink from it the drinking of thirsty camels).

The majority (al-Jumhūr) read "nuzuluhum" with a ḍammah on the zāy. Ibn Muḥayṣin, Kharija on the authority of Nafi', Nu'aym, Maḥbūb, Abu Zayd, Harun, 'Iṣma and 'Abbas, all on the authority of Abu 'Amr, read it with sukūn (no vowel on the zāy). "Nuzul" is the first thing a guest eats, and in it there is mockery of the disbelievers. A poet said:

*And when a tyrant came to us with his army as a guest, we made spears and sharp swords his nuzul.*

﴿يَوْمَ الدِّينِ﴾: that is, the Day of Recompense.

﴿نَحْنُ خَلَقْناكُمْ فَلَوْلا تُصَدِّقُونَ﴾ [Qur'an 56:57]: meaning, will you not affirm the return and acknowledge it, just as you acknowledged the first creation, which is their creation? Then He said: ﴿فَلَوْلا تُصَدِّقُونَ﴾ [Qur'an 56:57]: will you not affirm the return and acknowledge it, as you acknowledged? So it is an exhortation to affirmation.

﴿وَلَئِنْ سَأَلْتَهُمْ مَنْ خَلَقَهُمْ لَيَقُولُنَّ اللَّهُ﴾ [Qur'an 43:87]. Or: ﴿فَلَوْلا تُصَدِّقُونَ أَفَرَأَيْتُمْ﴾ [Qur'an 56:57–58]. Then He exhorted them to affirmation in the manner of rebuking them, by the sequence of proofs that necessitate affirmation. And a disbeliever said: Why should I affirm? It was said to him: Do you see such-and-such, which man is inherently disposed to acknowledge? So he said: ﴿أَفَرَأَيْتُمْ مَا تُمْنُونَ﴾ [Qur'an 56:58], which is the semen that comes out of man, since he has no action, will, or power in its creation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿تَخْلُقُونَهُ﴾ [Qur'an 56:59] means: you estimate it and form it. End of quote. So "khalq" is understood as estimating and forming, not as bringing into existence.

It is permissible for "a-antum" (Qur'an 56:59) to be the subject (mubtada'), with its predicate being "takhluqūnahu". The better view is that it is the agent of an elided verb, as if he said: "Do you create it?" When the verb was elided, the pronoun became detached. The "afara'aytum" here is explicitly followed by its first object. The occurrence of an interrogative clause in the position of the second object is as established in grammar, when it has the sense of "akhbirnī" (tell me).

After "am" there is a clause. It is said that "am" is munqaṭi'ah (disjunctive, not equalizing the hamzah), and not mu'ādilah (equalizing with the hamzah). This occurs in four places here, so that these are two interrogations: the answer to the first is "no" and the answer to the second is "yes". So "am" is estimated accordingly: "bal a-naḥnu al-khāliqūn" (Qur'an 56:59), and its answer is "yes".

Some grammarians said: "am" here is mu'ādilah for the hamzah, and what came as the predicate after "naḥnu" was brought for the sake of emphasis, since if he had said "am naḥnu", the mention of the predicate would have been unnecessary. The analogy of this is the answer to one who says: "Who is in the house?" — "Zayd is in the house" or "Zayd is in it". If he had confined the answer to "Zayd", it would have sufficed.

The majority read "mā tumnūna" with a ḍammah on the tā'. Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-Sammal read it with a fatḥah.

The majority read "qaddarnā" with a shaddah on the dāl. Ibn Kathir read it without the shaddah, meaning: We decreed and established, or arranged in precedence and succession, so the death of the world is not in one instant, but in an order that does not transgress.

It is said: "sabaqtuhu 'alā al-shay'": you overpowered him in it, defeated him in it, and did not enable him to attain it. The meaning of ﴿وَمَا نَحْنُ بِمَسْبُوقِينَ عَلى أَنْ نُبَدِّلَ أَمْثالَكُمْ﴾ [Qur'an 56:60] is: We are capable of that, and you cannot overcome us in it, if We wish that. Al-Ṭabarī said: The meaning is: We are capable — ﴿قَدَّرْنا بَيْنَكُمُ الْمَوْتَ﴾ [Qur'an 56:60] — ﴿عَلى أَنْ نُبَدِّلَ أَمْثالَكُمْ﴾: that is, by the death of a group and replacing it with another group, generation after generation. End of quote. So according to the first view, "'alā an nubaddila" is connected to "masbūqīn" (overcome), meaning: We are not outpaced. According to the second view, it is connected to "naḥnu qaddarnā".

﴿عَلى أَنْ نُبَدِّلَ أَمْثالَكُمْ﴾ [Qur'an 56:61]: "amthālakum" is the plural of "mithl". ﴿وَنُنْشِئَكُمْ فِي ما لا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ [Qur'an 56:61]: that is, in attributes: We are capable of annihilating you, bringing into being others like you, and changing your qualities in ways that your thought does not encompass. Al-Ḥasan said: From your being turned into apes and swine. He said this because the verse inclines toward a warning. It is also permissible for "amthālakum" to be the plural of "mithl" in the sense of "ṣifah" (attribute), meaning: We are capable of changing your attributes by which you are, in form and in character, and ﴿وَنُنْشِئَكُمْ﴾ [Qur'an 56:61] in attributes you do not know.

﴿وَلَقَدْ عَلِمْتُمُ النَّشْأَةَ الْأُولى﴾ [Qur'an 56:62]: that is, you knew that it is He who brought you into being; at first He brought a human being into existence. It is also said: it is the creation of Adam, that he was created from clay, and none of his offspring denies it.

﴿فَلَوْلا تَذَكَّرُونَ﴾ [Qur'an 56:62]: an exhortation to remembrance that leads to faith and acknowledgment of the afterlife creation. The majority read "tadhakkarūn" with a shaddah on the dhāl. Ṭalḥa read it without the shaddah with a ḍammah on the kāf. They said: This verse indicates the use of analogy (qiyās) and exhortation to it. End of quote. But this verse indicates only the analogy of what is more fitting (qiyās al-awlā), not all types of analogy.

you kindle?﴾ ﴿Is it you who produced its tree, or are We the producers?﴾ ﴿We made it a reminder and a provision for the travelers.﴾ ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Most Great.﴾ ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 75] ﴿And indeed it is a great oath, if you only knew﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 76] ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 77] ﴿in a Book well-guarded﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 78] ﴿which none touches except the purified﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 79] ﴿a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 80] ﴿Then is it this discourse that you disregard?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 81] ﴿And you make your provision that you deny?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 82] ﴿So why, when it reaches the throat﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 83] ﴿and you at that time are looking on﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 84] ﴿And We are nearer to him than you, but you do not see﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 85] ﴿So why not, if you are not to be recompensed﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 86] ﴿you return it, if you are truthful?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 87] ﴿And as for if he is of those brought near﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 88] ﴿then rest and sweet plants and a Garden of delight﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 89] ﴿And as for if he is of the companions of the right﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 90] ﴿then, "Peace be upon you from the companions of the right."﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 91] ﴿And as for if he is of the deniers, the astray﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 92] ﴿then a welcome of boiling water﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 93] ﴿and burning in Hellfire.﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 94] ﴿Indeed, this is the certain truth.﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 95] ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Most Great.﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 96]

(p-208) Al-yahmum: the intensely black. Al-hinth: al-Khattabi said that in the speech of the Arabs it means a heavy burden, and sin is likened to it. Al-Him: plural of ahyam and hayma'; al-hiyam is a thirst-causing disease that afflicts camels, so that they drink until they die, or become severely ill. He said:
"So I have become like the thirsty she-camel, neither does water heal her thirst, nor does her ailment end."

Al-him is also the plural of hiyam, which is sand, with a fatha on the ha', and this is the well-known form. Tha'lab said it is with a damma. He said: it is the sand that does not hold together. With a fatha, it is like sahab and suhub; then it was lightened and what was done to the plural of ahyam was done to it, by changing its damma into a kasra so that the ya' is sound; or with a damma, it is pluralized on the pattern fi'l like qurad and qird, then the damma of the ra' was made sukun so it became fi'l, then what was done to bid' was done to it. Amnā al-rajul: the man emitted the seed; and manna: he expelled it from his urethra. Al-muzn: the clouds. The poet said:
"No cloud has poured its rain, nor has land grown its herbage."

Awrā al-nar min al-zinad: I struck the fire from the firestriker; the firestriker itself is kindled. The zinad is two stones or a stone and an iron, or of wood, especially soft wood like al-markh, al-'ifar and al-kalh. The Arabs strike with two sticks, rubbing one against the other, and they call the upper one al-zand and the lower one al-zanda, likening them to the wheel and the hole. Aqwā al-rajul: he entered the wasteland, al-qawā, which is the desert, like asḥar: he entered the open desert. Aqwā also means he stayed days without eating anything. Aqwat al-dar: the house became desolate. The poet said:
"O abode of Mayya at al-'Aliya and al-Sanad, it has become desolate and long ages have passed over it."

Idhdhahana: he was soft and gentle, and was lax in matters that are not borne by the one who is lax. The poet said:
"Resolve and strength are better than compromise, and than softness and weakness."

Al-hulqum: the passage of food. Al-rawh: rest. Al-rayhan has been discussed in Surat al-Rahman.

(p-209) When he mentioned the state of the foremost, and followed them with the companions of the right, he mentioned the state of the companions of the left, saying: ﴿And the companions of the left﴾. The i'rab of a similar sentence has preceded, and in this interrogation is the magnification of their calamity.

﴿In scorching wind﴾: in the most intense heat. ﴿And boiling water﴾: water of extreme heat.

﴿And a shade of black smoke﴾: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Abu Malik, Ibn Zayd and the majority said: smoke. Ibn 'Abbas also said: it is the enclosure of the Fire surrounding its people, rising from every side until it shades them. Ibn Kaysan said: al-yahmum is one of the names of Jahannam. Ibn Zayd also said, and Ibn Buraydah: it is a black mountain in the Fire, to which the people of the Fire flee for refuge, and they find it the most severe and bitter of things.

﴿Neither cool nor pleasant﴾: two attributes of the shade, negated. It is called a shade though it is not like shades, and its coolness and benefit to one who takes refuge in it are negated.

﴿Nor pleasant﴾: a completion of the negation of the attribute of praise in it, and an annihilation of what might be imagined in the shade of finding relief in it in the intensity of heat; or a negation of the honor of one who finds relief in it. It is attributed to it metaphorically, and what is meant is they, i.e., they seek shade in it while they are humiliated. It may also be understood as a bad gathering place, not a means of attaining honor. The first attribute mentioned is the essential one, which is the shade, and that it is "of black smoke," so it is a part of the yahmum. Then He negated of it the attribute that would make it a shade, which is being neither cool nor pleasant. It is also permissible that ﴿neither cool nor pleasant﴾ be an attribute of yahmum, and it would then follow that the shade is described by that. The majority read ﴿neither cool nor pleasant﴾ with the genitive on both; Ibn Abi 'Abla read them with the nominative: i.e., it is neither cool nor pleasant, in the manner of his saying:
"So I spend the night, neither sinful nor deprived."
i.e., I am neither sinful.

﴿Indeed, they were before that﴾: i.e., in the worldly life, ﴿affluent﴾: in this is a condemnation of affluence and luxury in this world, and affluence is a path to idleness and abandoning reflection on the outcome.

﴿And they used to persist﴾: i.e., they continued and were constant, ﴿in the great violation﴾. Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said: it is polytheism, and this is the apparent meaning. It was said: what is contained in His saying: ﴿And they swore by Allah their most emphatic oaths﴾ [al-Nahl: 38] and so on, of denial of resurrection. But the next phrase rules this out: ﴿And they used to say﴾, for it is conjoined to what precedes it, and conjunction requires difference; so the great violation is polytheism. Their saying: ﴿When we have died and become dust and bones, will we indeed be resurrected?﴾ ﴿And our forefathers, the earlier ones?﴾ has been discussed previously in al-Saffat. Al-Zamakhshari repeated here his misconception, saying: If you ask, how is the conjunction to the pronoun in (la-mab'uthun) good without emphasis by "nahnu"? I say: it is good because of the intervening element, which is the interrogative hamza, just as it is good in His saying: ﴿Neither we nor our forefathers have associated﴾ [al-An'am: 148], because of the intervening la, which emphasizes the negation. End. We have refuted him here and there, returning to the view of the majority that they do not posit between the interrogative hamza and the conjunctive particle a verb, as in: ﴿Have they not travelled﴾ [Yusuf: 109], (p-210) nor a noun, as in (awa-aba'una); rather the wa and the fa are for conjoining what follows them to what precedes them, and the hamza in the underlying structure is posterior to the conjunctive particle. But since the interrogative has the front position in speech, it was placed first.

When He mentioned their questioning about resurrection in the manner of disbelief and denial, He commanded His Prophet ﷺ to inform them of the resurrection of all the world, the first and the last of them, for reckoning, and of what the deniers of resurrection will reach of punishment. Al-miqat: that by which a thing is timed, i.e., limited, i.e., to what the world is timed by, a known day; and the idafa is in the sense of min, like "a ring of iron." (Then indeed you): an address to the disbelievers of Quraysh, ﴿O you who are astray﴾ from guidance, ﴿and deniers﴾ of resurrection. It is also an address to whoever follows their course in this.

﴿Will surely eat from a tree of zaqqum﴾: the first "min" is for the beginning of the limit or for partitive; the second, if min zaqqum is an apposition, then min admits both possibilities; if it is not an apposition, then it is for specifying the kind, i.e., from a tree which is zaqqum. The majority read min shajar; 'Abd Allah read min shajarah.

﴿And fill their bellies from it﴾: the pronoun in minha refers to shajar, since it is a collective noun that may be feminine or masculine; and on the reading of 'Abd Allah, it is clear.

﴿فَشارِبُونَ عَلَيْهِ﴾ [Qur'an 56:55]. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is mentioned according to the wording of "tree" (shajar), just as it is made feminine according to its meaning in "minhā" [Qur'an 56:52]. He said: As for the one who reads "min shajaratin min zaqqūm" [Qur'an 56:52], he has made both pronouns refer to the tree. The second pronoun is mentioned in accordance with the interpretation of zaqqūm, because it explains the tree, and it is in its meaning. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The pronoun in "'alayhi" refers to the food that is eaten, or to the eating. End of quote. He did not make it refer to "shajar" (tree). Nafi', 'Asim and Hamza read "shurb" (drinking) with a ḍammah on the shīn, and it is a maṣdar (verbal noun). It is said that it is an ism (noun) for what is drunk. Mujahid and Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi read it with a kasrah, and it has the meaning of "mashrūb" (what is drunk); it is an ism, not a maṣdar, like "ṭaḥn" (grinding) and "ra'y" (pasturing). Al-A'raj, Ibn al-Musayyab, Shu'ayb ibn al-Ḥabḥāb, Malik ibn Dinar, Ibn Jurayj and the rest of the Seven read it with a fatḥah, and it is a regular maṣdar. (The Seven: the seven canonical readers of the Qur'an.)

"Al-Hīm" (the thirsty camels): Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrima and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said it is the plural of "ahyam", which is the camel afflicted by al-hiyām (a disease of extreme thirst), and we have explained it in the Mufradāt (the lexicon of Qur'anic vocabulary). It is also said that it is the plural of "hay'ā'" (feminine). It is also said that it is the plural of "hā'im" and "hā'ima" (wandering), and the plural of the pattern fā'il on the pattern fi'l is irregular, like "bādhil" and "bidhl", and "ā'idh" and "i'dh". The "hā'im" also comes from al-hiyām. Do you not see that when a camel is afflicted by that, it wanders aimlessly and goes away? Ibn 'Abbas and Sufyan said: "al-Hīm" are the sands that are not quenched by water. The disagreement regarding its singular has already passed: is it "al-Hiyām" with a fatḥah on the hā', or with a ḍammah?

The meaning is: He will impose upon them, from hunger, what compels them to eat the zaqqūm, which is like molten metal (al-muhl). When they fill their bellies with it, He will impose upon them, from thirst, what compels them to drink the ḥamīm (boiling water), which cuts their intestines, so they drink it as thirsty camels drink. Al-Zamakhshari said this.

He also said: If you say: how is it correct to conjoin "shāribūn" to "shāribūn", when they refer to the same persons and are two identical attributes, so it would be conjunction of a thing with itself? I say: They are not identical, because their being drinkers of the ḥamīm in the state of extreme heat and cutting of the intestines is an astonishing matter, and their drinking it in such a way, as thirsty camels drink water, is also an astonishing matter. Thus they are two different attributes. End of quote.

The fā' (then) indicates sequence between the two drinkings: when they first became thirsty, they drank of the ḥamīm, thinking that it would quench their thirst, but the thirst increased because of the heat of the ḥamīm. So they drank after it a drinking by which they never attain satisfaction, and that is like the drinking of the thirsty camels. Thus these are two drinkings of ḥamīm, not one drinking; its attributes differ, so it is conjoined, and the intended point is the attribute. The object from which they drink in ﴿فَشارِبُونَ شُرْبَ الْهِيمِ﴾ is elided because the meaning is understood. Its estimated form is: "fa-shāribūna minhu shurba al-hīm" (so you will drink from it the drinking of thirsty camels).

The majority (al-Jumhūr) read "nuzuluhum" with a ḍammah on the zāy. Ibn Muḥayṣin, Kharija on the authority of Nafi', Nu'aym, Maḥbūb, Abu Zayd, Harun, 'Iṣma and 'Abbas, all on the authority of Abu 'Amr, read it with sukūn (no vowel on the zāy). "Nuzul" is the first thing a guest eats, and in it there is mockery of the disbelievers. A poet said:

*And when a tyrant came to us with his army as a guest, we made spears and sharp swords his nuzul.*

﴿يَوْمَ الدِّينِ﴾: that is, the Day of Recompense.

﴿نَحْنُ خَلَقْناكُمْ فَلَوْلا تُصَدِّقُونَ﴾ [Qur'an 56:57]: meaning, will you not affirm the return and acknowledge it, just as you acknowledged the first creation, which is their creation? Then He said: ﴿فَلَوْلا تُصَدِّقُونَ﴾ [Qur'an 56:57]: will you not affirm the return and acknowledge it, as you acknowledged? So it is an exhortation to affirmation.

﴿وَلَئِنْ سَأَلْتَهُمْ مَنْ خَلَقَهُمْ لَيَقُولُنَّ اللَّهُ﴾ [Qur'an 43:87]. Or: ﴿فَلَوْلا تُصَدِّقُونَ أَفَرَأَيْتُمْ﴾ [Qur'an 56:57–58]. Then He exhorted them to affirmation in the manner of rebuking them, by the sequence of proofs that necessitate affirmation. And a disbeliever said: Why should I affirm? It was said to him: Do you see such-and-such, which man is inherently disposed to acknowledge? So he said: ﴿أَفَرَأَيْتُمْ مَا تُمْنُونَ﴾ [Qur'an 56:58], which is the semen that comes out of man, since he has no action, will, or power in its creation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿تَخْلُقُونَهُ﴾ [Qur'an 56:59] means: you estimate it and form it. End of quote. So "khalq" is understood as estimating and forming, not as bringing into existence.

It is permissible for "a-antum" (Qur'an 56:59) to be the subject (mubtada'), with its predicate being "takhluqūnahu". The better view is that it is the agent of an elided verb, as if he said: "Do you create it?" When the verb was elided, the pronoun became detached. The "afara'aytum" here is explicitly followed by its first object. The occurrence of an interrogative clause in the position of the second object is as established in grammar, when it has the sense of "akhbirnī" (tell me).

After "am" there is a clause. It is said that "am" is munqaṭi'ah (disjunctive, not equalizing the hamzah), and not mu'ādilah (equalizing with the hamzah). This occurs in four places here, so that these are two interrogations: the answer to the first is "no" and the answer to the second is "yes". So "am" is estimated accordingly: "bal a-naḥnu al-khāliqūn" (Qur'an 56:59), and its answer is "yes".

Some grammarians said: "am" here is mu'ādilah for the hamzah, and what came as the predicate after "naḥnu" was brought for the sake of emphasis, since if he had said "am naḥnu", the mention of the predicate would have been unnecessary. The analogy of this is the answer to one who says: "Who is in the house?" — "Zayd is in the house" or "Zayd is in it". If he had confined the answer to "Zayd", it would have sufficed.

The majority read "mā tumnūna" with a ḍammah on the tā'. Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-Sammal read it with a fatḥah.

The majority read "qaddarnā" with a shaddah on the dāl. Ibn Kathir read it without the shaddah, meaning: We decreed and established, or arranged in precedence and succession, so the death of the world is not in one instant, but in an order that does not transgress.

It is said: "sabaqtuhu 'alā al-shay'": you overpowered him in it, defeated him in it, and did not enable him to attain it. The meaning of ﴿وَمَا نَحْنُ بِمَسْبُوقِينَ عَلى أَنْ نُبَدِّلَ أَمْثالَكُمْ﴾ [Qur'an 56:60] is: We are capable of that, and you cannot overcome us in it, if We wish that. Al-Ṭabarī said: The meaning is: We are capable — ﴿قَدَّرْنا بَيْنَكُمُ الْمَوْتَ﴾ [Qur'an 56:60] — ﴿عَلى أَنْ نُبَدِّلَ أَمْثالَكُمْ﴾: that is, by the death of a group and replacing it with another group, generation after generation. End of quote. So according to the first view, "'alā an nubaddila" is connected to "masbūqīn" (overcome), meaning: We are not outpaced. According to the second view, it is connected to "naḥnu qaddarnā".

﴿عَلى أَنْ نُبَدِّلَ أَمْثالَكُمْ﴾ [Qur'an 56:61]: "amthālakum" is the plural of "mithl". ﴿وَنُنْشِئَكُمْ فِي ما لا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ [Qur'an 56:61]: that is, in attributes: We are capable of annihilating you, bringing into being others like you, and changing your qualities in ways that your thought does not encompass. Al-Ḥasan said: From your being turned into apes and swine. He said this because the verse inclines toward a warning. It is also permissible for "amthālakum" to be the plural of "mithl" in the sense of "ṣifah" (attribute), meaning: We are capable of changing your attributes by which you are, in form and in character, and ﴿وَنُنْشِئَكُمْ﴾ [Qur'an 56:61] in attributes you do not know.

﴿وَلَقَدْ عَلِمْتُمُ النَّشْأَةَ الْأُولى﴾ [Qur'an 56:62]: that is, you knew that it is He who brought you into being; at first He brought a human being into existence. It is also said: it is the creation of Adam, that he was created from clay, and none of his offspring denies it.

﴿فَلَوْلا تَذَكَّرُونَ﴾ [Qur'an 56:62]: an exhortation to remembrance that leads to faith and acknowledgment of the afterlife creation. The majority read "tadhakkarūn" with a shaddah on the dhāl. Ṭalḥa read it without the shaddah with a ḍammah on the kāf. They said: This verse indicates the use of analogy (qiyās) and exhortation to it. End of quote. But this verse indicates only the analogy of what is more fitting (qiyās al-awlā), not all types of analogy.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 56, verses 75–96 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Have you considered what you sow?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 63]: that is, what you scatter in the earth and sow. ﴿Is it you who cause it to grow?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 64]: that is, a crop that becomes complete and grows until it can be benefited from. Al-huttam is the dry, crumbled thing that has no grain from which one can benefit.

﴿So you would be left wondering﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 65]. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah said: "You would be amazed." 'Ikrimah said: "You would blame one another." Al-Hasan said: "You would regret." Ibn Zayd said: "You would be stricken with grief." All of this is interpretation by way of the necessary consequence (tafsir bi-l-lazim). The meaning of tafakkahun is that you cast off fukahah (amusement) from yourselves, and fukahah is joy. A man who is fakih is one whose soul is at ease and who is not concerned with anything. Tafakkaha belongs to the same family as takharraja and tahawwaba.

The majority read ﴿fazaltum﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 65] with a fatha on the ẓa' and a single lam. Abu Haywah and Abu Bakr, in the transmission of al-Qaykiyy from him, read it with a kasra. This is like their saying massat, with a fatha and a kasra on the mim, which al-Thawri related from Ibn Mas'ud, and which also came down from al-A'mash. 'Abd Allah and al-Jahdari read fazhilltum on the original form, with a kasra on the lam. Al-Jahdari also read it with a fatha. The well-known reading is zalilt with a kasra. The majority read ﴿tafakkahun﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 65]; Abu Haram read it with a nun in place of the ha'. Ibn Khalawayh said: tafakkaha means "he wondered," and tafakkana means "he regretted."

﴿Indeed we are burdened with debt﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 66]: before it there is an omitted element, meaning they say. The majority read innā; al-A'mash, al-Jahdari and Abu Bakr read a'innā with two hamzas. ﴿We are burdened with debt﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 66] means: we are tormented by ghuram, which is the most severe punishment. A poet said:

*If He punishes, it will be a ghuram; and if He gives abundantly, He does not care.*

Or it means: we are charged with the cost of expenditure, since our wealth has gone. Ghirama al-rajul means he incurred debt, and aghramtuhu means I made him incur it.

﴿Rather, we are deprived﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 67]: mahdudun, meaning we have no share of goodness.

﴿The water that you drink﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 68]: this description makes the description as "sweet" unnecessary. Do you not see its opposite, which is the salty (ujaj)? The lam entered in ﴿We could make it into debris﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 65] and was dropped in His saying ﴿We made it salty﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 70], and both are eloquent. Al-Zamakhshari went on at length about the justification for this, and its summary is this: when a particle is used in a place and becomes known and famous in that place, it may be omitted because its matter is well known. The lam is a marker of the connection of the second sentence to the first, so it may be omitted, relying on the listener's knowledge. In his speech it is mentioned that the second was prevented because the first was prevented, but this is not as he stated. This is only the view of weak grammarians (al-mu'rabin). What Sibawayh stated is that it is a particle for what would have occurred, because the first occurred. The view of those weak grammarians is refuted by their own saying: "If he were a human, he would be an animal," since animality is not prevented merely because humanity is prevented. Then he said: It is possible to say that this lam necessarily conveys the meaning of emphasis, and it was introduced into the verse about food and not the verse about drink, to indicate that the matter of food takes precedence over the matter of drink, and that the threat of its loss is more severe and more difficult, since drink is only needed as a secondary to food. For this reason the verse about food was placed before the verse about drink.

The apparent meaning of ﴿its tree﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 72] is the tree from which fire is struck. It was said that the tree refers to the fire itself, as if He were saying: its type or its kind, so He used "tree" as a metaphor for that. This is a far-fetched view.

﴿We made it a reminder﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 73]: that is, a reminder of the fire of Hell, ﴿and a provision for the wayfarers﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 73]: that is, those who alight in the qaw, which is the desert. It was said: for travellers, which is close to what came before. The saying of Ibn Zayd, "the hungry," is very weak. He mentioned first the benefits of the fire that are more important and more emphatic than reminding of the fire of Hell, and then followed it with its benefit in this world. These four matters, which Allah the Exalted mentioned and made them acknowledge, concern the creation of human beings and what sustains their life, namely food and drink. Fire is among the greatest proofs of resurrection, since in it there is transition from one thing to another and the bringing into being of one thing from another. For this reason, at the end of the passage He commanded glorifying Him, exalted above what the disbelievers say. He described Himself as the Mighty, since whoever has these acts demonstrates His greatness, His majesty, and His singularity in creation and origination.

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ ﴿And indeed it is an oath, if you only knew, a great one﴾ ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾ ﴿in a Book well-guarded﴾ ﴿which none touches except the purified﴾ ﴿a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ ﴿Is it this discourse that you are scornful of?﴾ ﴿And you make your provision that you deny?﴾ ﴿Why, then, when it reaches the throat﴾ ﴿and you at that time are looking on﴾ ﴿and We are nearer to him than you, but you do not see﴾ ﴿Why, then, if you are not to be recompensed﴾ ﴿would you not bring it back, if you are truthful?﴾ ﴿As for if he is of those brought near﴾ ﴿then rest and provision and a Garden of bliss﴾ ﴿And as for if he is of the companions of the right﴾ ﴿then peace be upon you from the companions of the right﴾ ﴿And as for if he is of the deniers, the astray﴾ ﴿then a welcome of boiling water﴾ ﴿and roasting in Hellfire﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is the certain truth﴾ ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 75–96].

[p-212] The majority read ﴿fa-la uqsimu﴾. It was said that la is an extra, emphasizing particle, like its use in His saying ﴿so that the People of the Book may know﴾ [al-Hadid: 29], and the meaning is: "so I swear." It was also said that the negation is omitted, meaning: there is no truth to what the disbelievers say. Then he began with "uqsimu" ("I swear"). This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and some grammarians, but it is not permissible, because that would involve omitting the subject and predicate of la, and it is not an answer to a questioner who asked, so that it could be allowed, like the saying "la" in response to one who asks: "Is there anyone in the house?" It was also said that it is an emphatic particle of intensification, similar to an opening phrase of speech, resembling it in the oath except that it is common in speech and in other than oaths, and from it is the line:

*So no, by the father of its enemies, I will not betray it.*

My preferred view is that it is a lam whose fatha was prolonged, from which an alif was produced, like His saying:

*I seek refuge in Allah from the scorpion.*

Although this is rare, its counterpart appears in His saying ﴿so make hearts incline toward them from among the people﴾ [Ibrahim: 37], with a ya' after the hamza, which is in the reading of Hisham. So the meaning is: "then I swear," as in the reading of al-Hasan and 'Isa. Abu al-Fath explained al-Hasan's reading as based on an omitted subject, meaning "then indeed I swear," and al-Zamakhshari followed him in this. They went this way because it is a present-tense verb, and there is disagreement about swearing upon it. What Ibn 'Usfur and others chose is that a present-tense verb cannot be the object of an oath, so they had to treat the imperfect as the predicate of an omitted subject, making the sentence a nominal sentence, and then swearing upon it. Some grammarians held that swearing upon a present-tense verb is permissible, and this is what I choose. So you say: "By Allah, Zayd will indeed go out," and the poet's saying supports this:

*My Lord knows that my house is spacious.*

Al-Zamakhshari said, regarding al-Hasan's reading: the lam cannot be the lam of oath, for two reasons. One is that it should be accompanied by the emphatic nun, and omitting it is weak and ugly. The second is that la af'alanna in the answer of the oath is for the future, while the verb of the oath must be for the present. End of quotation. As for the first reason, there is disagreement about it: what he said is the view of the Basrans, while the Kufans prefer that, but they allow the two to alternate, so they permit "la adribanna Zaydan" and "adribanna 'Amran." As for the second reason, it is correct, but it is the one that we find preferable, that the lam in "la uqsimu" is the lam of oath, and "uqsimu" is a present-tense verb, and the oath may be an answer to an oath, as He said: ﴿And they will surely swear, "We intended nothing but good"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 107]. The lam in ﴿wa la yahlifunna﴾ [al-Tawbah: 107] is the answer to an oath, and it is an oath. But since their swearing was not present but future, the nun was required, since it makes the imperfect unambiguously future.

The majority read ﴿bi-mawaqi'i﴾ in the plural. 'Umar, 'Abd Allah, Ibn 'Abbas, the people of Madinah, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read [p-214] bi-mawqi'i in the singular, intending the plural. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, Mujahid and others said: they are the stars of the Qur'an, which were sent down upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. This view is supported by His saying ﴿Indeed, it is a Qur'an﴾, since the pronoun refers to what is understood from His saying ﴿the positions of the stars﴾, meaning the stars of the Qur'an. It was also said: the stars are the planets and their positions. Mujahid and Abu 'Ubaydah said: at their rising and setting. Qatadah said: their positions are their places in the sky. Al-Hasan said: their positions are at the time of their falling on the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: at their dispersal after being shot as meteors. Whoever interpreted "the stars" as the planets makes the pronoun in "innahu" explained by the context of the speech, like His saying ﴿until it was hidden by the veil﴾ [Sad: 32].

In His swearing by the positions of the stars there is a secret in the glorifying of that which we do not know, and He magnified it greatly, saying: ﴿And indeed it is an oath, if you only knew, a great one﴾. The sentence sworn to is His saying ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾, and the oath is separated from its answer. The apparent view is that it is a parenthetical insertion between them, and in it there is a parenthetical insertion between the attribute and the qualified noun by His saying "if you only knew." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: ﴿And indeed it is an oath﴾ is an emphasis on the matter and an alerting from the one sworn by, and this is not a parenthesis between the two statements. Rather, this is a meaning intended for its gravity, and the parenthesis is only His saying "if you only knew." End of quotation. Karim (noble) is a description of praise that negates from it what is not fitting for it. Al-Zamakhshari said: "karim" means good and pleasing in its kind among books, or beneficial and of abundant benefits, or noble before Allah the Exalted.

﴿In a Book well-guarded﴾: that is, protected. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: it is the Book that is in the heaven. 'Ikrimah said: the Torah and the Gospel, as if He said: its nobility and honour were mentioned in a well-guarded Book, so the meaning according to this is citing the revealed books. It was also said: ﴿in a well-guarded Book﴾ means in the codices of the Muslims, protected from alteration and change, and at that time there were no codices, so this is a report of the unseen.

The apparent view is that His saying ﴿which none touches except the purified﴾ is a description of the noble Qur'an, so the purified are the angels. It was also said that ﴿which none touches﴾ is a description of the well-guarded Book. If the Book is the one in heaven, then the purified are also the angels, meaning none other than them can access it. Likewise according to the view of 'Ikrimah, they are the angels. If by the Book well-guarded is meant the written pages, then the meaning is that it should not be touched except by one who is in a state of purity among people. If the purified are the angels, then "none touches" is a negation, and the negated is supported by the reading of 'Abd Allah, "what touches it." If by them is meant those who are purified from disbelief and major impurity, then it may be a pure negation, and its ruling is that none touches it except the purified, even though one who is not purified may touch it, as in the hadith: "Its trees are not to be cut," meaning this is the ruling, even though cutting does occur. It may also be a negation intended as a prohibition, so the damma on the sin is an inflection. It may also be a prohibition, in which case, if the jussive were made explicit, it would appear, but since it was assimilated, it is jussive in estimation, and the damma on it is for the sake of the damma of the ha', as in the hadith: "Indeed we did not return it to you," where it is jussive and is jussive, and Sibawayh did not record in such cases of the assimilated jussive connected to the ha' of a masculine pronoun anything except the damma. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the view that "none touches" is a prohibition is a weak view, because if it is a statement, it stands in the position of an attribute, and His saying after that, "a revelation," is an attribute. If we make it a prohibition, its meaning becomes foreign, inserted between the attributes, and that is not good in describing speech, so consider it carefully. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud is "ma yamassuhu," and this strengthens what I preferred, that the statement whose meaning is that its worth and rank require that none touch it except one who is pure. End of quotation.

Abu Hayyan's commentary on Surah al-Waqi'ah (56:75–96), part 2 of 2

It is not necessary that *tanzīlun* (a sending down) be a qualifier (ṣifa, adjective). It may instead be the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada', the topic), in which case *lā yamassuhu* (﴿none touch it﴾) can be read as a prohibition (nahy). Here the scholars mention the ruling on touching the mushaf (the written copy of the Qur'an), which is discussed in jurisprudence (fiqh). There is nothing in the verse that proves a prohibition of this.

The majority read *al-mutahharūn* (﴿the purified﴾) as a passive participle (ism maf'ul) from *tahhara* in the intensive form. ʿĪsā read it likewise but in the form *aṭhara* (without doubling). It is also narrated from Nāfiʿ and Abū ʿAmr. Salmān al-Fārisī read *al-muṭahharūn* with a light ṭāʾ, a doubled hāʾ, and a kasra, as an active participle (ism fāʿil) from *taharra*, meaning "those who purify themselves." It is also narrated from him *al-muṭṭahharūn* with both letters doubled. Its original form is *al-mutaṭahharūn*, and the tāʾ was assimilated into the ṭāʾ (idgham, assimilation of consonants). This is narrated from al-Ḥasan and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAwf. It was also read *al-mutaṭahharūn*. It was read *tanzīlan* with a fatḥa, meaning "it was sent down, a sending down."

In ﴿Then is it of this discourse﴾, the pointer refers to the Qur'an. *Antum* (you) is addressed to the disbelievers. *Mudhinūn* (﴿disputing/being lax﴾): Ibn ʿAbbās said: "slackening in what is not lawful." He also said: "denying."

﴿And you make your provision﴾: that is, instead of thanking Allah for what He has provided you, by sending down the Qur'an upon you, you respond with denial. In other words, you put denial in the place of thanks. From this meaning is the verse of the rajaz poet:

*In place of the thanks of the people for favours,*
*is the branding of healthy camels and the gouging of eyes.*

ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās read *wa-tajʿalūna shukrakum* (and you make your thanks), and this is by way of explanation, since it differs from the written text (the rasm). Al-Haytham ibn ʿAdī related that in the dialect of the Azd Shanūʾa, *mā razaqa fulānun fulānan* means "what so-and-so thanked so-and-so for." It was said: the verse was revealed concerning the star-risings (anwāʾ) and attributing the watering (of the rain) to them, while *al-rizq* means the rain. The meaning is: what Allah provides you from the unseen. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: the commentators agreed that the verse is a rebuke to those who speak of rain, saying "this is by the star-rising of such and such," "this is by the star-rising of the Lion," "this is by the star-rising of Orion," and other such things.

The majority read *tukadhdhibūn* (you deny) from *takdhīb* (denial). ʿAlī and al-Mufaḍḍal from ʿĀṣim read it from *kadhib* (lying). The meaning of the first (denial) is that it is not from Allah, that is, the Qur'an or the rain, since they attribute that to the stars. The meaning of the second (lying) is their saying: the Qur'an is sorcery and fabrication, and the rain comes from the star-risings.

﴿Then why, when it reaches the throat, and you are at that moment looking on…﴾. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the arrangement of the verse is: "then why do you not send it back when it reaches the throat, if you are not held to account?" The second *falawlā* is repeated for emphasis, and the pronoun in *tarji'ūnahā* (you return it) refers to the soul (nafs). Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it is a halt at a point of deficiency, which requires considering that Allah is the owner of everything. *Antum* (you) is a reference to all of humankind. *Ḥīna'idhin* (at that time): at the time when it reaches the throat. *Tanẓurūn* (you look on): that is, at the one who is dying. ʿĪsā read *ḥīna'idhin* with a kasra on the nūn, following the vowel of the hamza in *idh*.

﴿And We are nearer to him than you, by knowledge and power﴾, ﴿but you do not see﴾: from the insight of the heart. Or (*aqrab*, nearer) means: Our angels and Our messengers. ﴿But you do not see﴾: from the sight of the eye.

Then the halt and the consideration return a second time with the wording of restriction. *Al-Madīn* means "one who is owned." Al-Akhṭal said:

*She raised me, and my upbringing was in her lap, the son of a slave-woman.*

It was said: "the son of a slave-girl," describing a slave, the son of a female slave. The end of the verse is:

*You see him upon a mule, going about.*

The meaning is: why do you not send back the soul that has reached the throat, if you are not owned and not subdued?

﴿If you are truthful﴾ in your nullifying and disbelief in the One who gives life and causes death, who originates and restores. This is because they held that the Qur'an is sorcery and fabrication, and that the rain that falls is by such and such a star-rising. That is a nullifying of the Creator and a rendering Him powerless.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: His saying *tarji'ūnahā* (you return it) stands in the place of its answer (the apodosis), and the explanations required by the restrictions (of the conditions), and *idhā* in His saying *falawlā idhā* (then why, when), and the repeated *in* (if). Some speech carries other speech, by way of brevity and economy. End of quotation. I say: *idhā* is not conditional. It does not stand in the place of its answer, rather it is an adverbial, non-conditional circumstantial phrase governed by the omitted *tarji'ūnahā* after *falawlā*, because *tarji'ūnahā* in the second restriction indicates it. So the first restriction came restricted to the time of reaching the throat, and the second restriction came conditional upon the negation of their being owned, and they cannot return it, since their being owned is existent. Thus they are subdued, with no power.

﴿But if he is of those brought near﴾, that is, the one who has died, ﴿those brought near﴾: they are the foremost.

The majority read *fa-rawḥun* (then rest) with a fatḥa on the rāʾ. ʿĀʾisha, from the Prophet (ﷺ), Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, Nūḥ al-Qāriʾ, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Ashhab, Shuʿayb ibn al-Ḥabḥāb, Sulaymān al-Taymī, al-Rabīʿ ibn Khaytham, Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī, Abū ʿImrān al-Jawnī, al-Kalbī, Fayyāḍ, ʿUbayd, ʿAbd al-Wārith from Abū ʿAmr, Yaʿqūb ibn Ṣayyān, Zayd, and Ruways from him read it with a ḍamma.

al-Ḥasan said: *al-rawḥ* means mercy, because it is like life for the one who is shown mercy. He also said: his spirit departs in a sweet basil (rayḥān). It was said: *al-rawḥ* means remaining (baqāʾ), that is, both of these are for him together: eternity with provision.

Mujāhid said: *al-rayḥān* means provision. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: rest. Abū al-ʿĀliya, Qatāda, and al-Ḥasan also said: *al-rayḥān* is this well-known plant of the world, and the one brought near receives a sweet basil from Paradise. al-Khalīl said: it is the container of every good herb in which the first buds of blossom appear.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said about al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn, may Allah be pleased with them both: "They are my two sweet basils of this world."

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: *al-rayḥān* is that with which souls are delighted. ﴿Then rest﴾: then peace. *Fa-nuzulun*: the fā' is the answer to *ammā*, which came before it. *Ammā* is in the sense of a condition: "if he is of those brought near," "if he is of the companions of the right," "if he is of the denying, the astray," are conditions. When two conditions come together, the answer belongs to the first of them. The answer to the second is omitted, and for this reason the verb of the condition is in the past form, or accompanied by *lam*. The answer of *ammā* has taken its place. This is the position of Sībawayh. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī held that the fā' is the answer of *in*, and the answer of *ammā* is omitted, and he has a view agreeing with Sībawayh's position. al-Akhfash held that the fā' is the answer of *ammā* and the condition together. We have refuted these two positions in our book called *al-Tadhyīl wa-al-Takmīl fī Sharḥ al-Tashīl*.

The address in this is to the Messenger (ﷺ), meaning: you do not see among them, O Muhammad, except safety from punishment. Then for every one who takes heed from his community (ﷺ) there is a statement addressed to him: ﴿of the companions of the right﴾.

al-Ṭabarī said: the meaning is: peace to you, you who are of the companions of the right. Others said: the meaning is: it will be said to them, "Safe for you, because you are of the companions of the right." It was said: peace to you, O companion of the right, from your brothers, the companions of the right, that is, they greet you, like His saying: ﴿except the saying "Peace, peace"﴾ [al-Wāqiʿa 26].

The denying, astray ones are the companions of the left (*al-mash'ama*), the companions of the left hand.

The majority read *wa-taṣliyatun* (and burning) in the nominative, in conjunction with *fa-nuzulun*. Aḥmad ibn Mūsā, al-Minqarī, and al-Luʾluʾī from Abū ʿAmr read it in the genitive, in conjunction with *min ḥamīm* (of boiling water).

When the account of their conditions and where each category of them ends up has concluded, He confirmed that with His saying: ﴿Indeed, this﴾, that is, indeed this report mentioned in this surah ﴿is the truth of certainty﴾. It was said: this is from the construction of two synonyms for the sake of emphasis, as you say: "this is the certainty of certainty" and "the correctness of correctness," meaning that it is the ultimate in that, so the two have one meaning, and it is joined for emphasis. It was said: this is from the construction of a described thing with its description, making "the truth" distinct from "the certainty," that is, the established, the certainly known.

When the three categories had been mentioned at length, He, Exalted is He, commanded him to declare Him free from what does not befit Him of attributes. When He repeated the division briefly, He likewise commanded him to declare Him free and to glorify Him, to devote himself to worshipping his Lord, and to turn away from the sayings of the disbelievers who deny the Resurrection, the Reckoning, and the Recompense.

It appears that *sabbiḥ* (glorify) is transitive sometimes by itself, as in His saying: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Aʿlā 1], and *yusabbiḥūhu*; and sometimes by a preposition, as in His saying: ﴿So glorify with the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾. The word *al-ʿaẓīm* (the Mighty) may be a qualifier of *ism* (name), and it may be a qualifier of *rabbika* (your Lord).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 56, verses 75–96 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Have you considered what you sow?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 63]: that is, what you scatter in the earth and sow. ﴿Is it you who cause it to grow?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 64]: that is, a crop that becomes complete and grows until it can be benefited from. Al-huttam is the dry, crumbled thing that has no grain from which one can benefit.

﴿So you would be left wondering﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 65]. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah said: "You would be amazed." 'Ikrimah said: "You would blame one another." Al-Hasan said: "You would regret." Ibn Zayd said: "You would be stricken with grief." All of this is interpretation by way of the necessary consequence (tafsir bi-l-lazim). The meaning of tafakkahun is that you cast off fukahah (amusement) from yourselves, and fukahah is joy. A man who is fakih is one whose soul is at ease and who is not concerned with anything. Tafakkaha belongs to the same family as takharraja and tahawwaba.

The majority read ﴿fazaltum﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 65] with a fatha on the ẓa' and a single lam. Abu Haywah and Abu Bakr, in the transmission of al-Qaykiyy from him, read it with a kasra. This is like their saying massat, with a fatha and a kasra on the mim, which al-Thawri related from Ibn Mas'ud, and which also came down from al-A'mash. 'Abd Allah and al-Jahdari read fazhilltum on the original form, with a kasra on the lam. Al-Jahdari also read it with a fatha. The well-known reading is zalilt with a kasra. The majority read ﴿tafakkahun﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 65]; Abu Haram read it with a nun in place of the ha'. Ibn Khalawayh said: tafakkaha means "he wondered," and tafakkana means "he regretted."

﴿Indeed we are burdened with debt﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 66]: before it there is an omitted element, meaning they say. The majority read innā; al-A'mash, al-Jahdari and Abu Bakr read a'innā with two hamzas. ﴿We are burdened with debt﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 66] means: we are tormented by ghuram, which is the most severe punishment. A poet said:

*If He punishes, it will be a ghuram; and if He gives abundantly, He does not care.*

Or it means: we are charged with the cost of expenditure, since our wealth has gone. Ghirama al-rajul means he incurred debt, and aghramtuhu means I made him incur it.

﴿Rather, we are deprived﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 67]: mahdudun, meaning we have no share of goodness.

﴿The water that you drink﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 68]: this description makes the description as "sweet" unnecessary. Do you not see its opposite, which is the salty (ujaj)? The lam entered in ﴿We could make it into debris﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 65] and was dropped in His saying ﴿We made it salty﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 70], and both are eloquent. Al-Zamakhshari went on at length about the justification for this, and its summary is this: when a particle is used in a place and becomes known and famous in that place, it may be omitted because its matter is well known. The lam is a marker of the connection of the second sentence to the first, so it may be omitted, relying on the listener's knowledge. In his speech it is mentioned that the second was prevented because the first was prevented, but this is not as he stated. This is only the view of weak grammarians (al-mu'rabin). What Sibawayh stated is that it is a particle for what would have occurred, because the first occurred. The view of those weak grammarians is refuted by their own saying: "If he were a human, he would be an animal," since animality is not prevented merely because humanity is prevented. Then he said: It is possible to say that this lam necessarily conveys the meaning of emphasis, and it was introduced into the verse about food and not the verse about drink, to indicate that the matter of food takes precedence over the matter of drink, and that the threat of its loss is more severe and more difficult, since drink is only needed as a secondary to food. For this reason the verse about food was placed before the verse about drink.

The apparent meaning of ﴿its tree﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 72] is the tree from which fire is struck. It was said that the tree refers to the fire itself, as if He were saying: its type or its kind, so He used "tree" as a metaphor for that. This is a far-fetched view.

﴿We made it a reminder﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 73]: that is, a reminder of the fire of Hell, ﴿and a provision for the wayfarers﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 73]: that is, those who alight in the qaw, which is the desert. It was said: for travellers, which is close to what came before. The saying of Ibn Zayd, "the hungry," is very weak. He mentioned first the benefits of the fire that are more important and more emphatic than reminding of the fire of Hell, and then followed it with its benefit in this world. These four matters, which Allah the Exalted mentioned and made them acknowledge, concern the creation of human beings and what sustains their life, namely food and drink. Fire is among the greatest proofs of resurrection, since in it there is transition from one thing to another and the bringing into being of one thing from another. For this reason, at the end of the passage He commanded glorifying Him, exalted above what the disbelievers say. He described Himself as the Mighty, since whoever has these acts demonstrates His greatness, His majesty, and His singularity in creation and origination.

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ ﴿And indeed it is an oath, if you only knew, a great one﴾ ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾ ﴿in a Book well-guarded﴾ ﴿which none touches except the purified﴾ ﴿a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ ﴿Is it this discourse that you are scornful of?﴾ ﴿And you make your provision that you deny?﴾ ﴿Why, then, when it reaches the throat﴾ ﴿and you at that time are looking on﴾ ﴿and We are nearer to him than you, but you do not see﴾ ﴿Why, then, if you are not to be recompensed﴾ ﴿would you not bring it back, if you are truthful?﴾ ﴿As for if he is of those brought near﴾ ﴿then rest and provision and a Garden of bliss﴾ ﴿And as for if he is of the companions of the right﴾ ﴿then peace be upon you from the companions of the right﴾ ﴿And as for if he is of the deniers, the astray﴾ ﴿then a welcome of boiling water﴾ ﴿and roasting in Hellfire﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is the certain truth﴾ ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 75–96].

[p-212] The majority read ﴿fa-la uqsimu﴾. It was said that la is an extra, emphasizing particle, like its use in His saying ﴿so that the People of the Book may know﴾ [al-Hadid: 29], and the meaning is: "so I swear." It was also said that the negation is omitted, meaning: there is no truth to what the disbelievers say. Then he began with "uqsimu" ("I swear"). This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and some grammarians, but it is not permissible, because that would involve omitting the subject and predicate of la, and it is not an answer to a questioner who asked, so that it could be allowed, like the saying "la" in response to one who asks: "Is there anyone in the house?" It was also said that it is an emphatic particle of intensification, similar to an opening phrase of speech, resembling it in the oath except that it is common in speech and in other than oaths, and from it is the line:

*So no, by the father of its enemies, I will not betray it.*

My preferred view is that it is a lam whose fatha was prolonged, from which an alif was produced, like His saying:

*I seek refuge in Allah from the scorpion.*

Although this is rare, its counterpart appears in His saying ﴿so make hearts incline toward them from among the people﴾ [Ibrahim: 37], with a ya' after the hamza, which is in the reading of Hisham. So the meaning is: "then I swear," as in the reading of al-Hasan and 'Isa. Abu al-Fath explained al-Hasan's reading as based on an omitted subject, meaning "then indeed I swear," and al-Zamakhshari followed him in this. They went this way because it is a present-tense verb, and there is disagreement about swearing upon it. What Ibn 'Usfur and others chose is that a present-tense verb cannot be the object of an oath, so they had to treat the imperfect as the predicate of an omitted subject, making the sentence a nominal sentence, and then swearing upon it. Some grammarians held that swearing upon a present-tense verb is permissible, and this is what I choose. So you say: "By Allah, Zayd will indeed go out," and the poet's saying supports this:

*My Lord knows that my house is spacious.*

Al-Zamakhshari said, regarding al-Hasan's reading: the lam cannot be the lam of oath, for two reasons. One is that it should be accompanied by the emphatic nun, and omitting it is weak and ugly. The second is that la af'alanna in the answer of the oath is for the future, while the verb of the oath must be for the present. End of quotation. As for the first reason, there is disagreement about it: what he said is the view of the Basrans, while the Kufans prefer that, but they allow the two to alternate, so they permit "la adribanna Zaydan" and "adribanna 'Amran." As for the second reason, it is correct, but it is the one that we find preferable, that the lam in "la uqsimu" is the lam of oath, and "uqsimu" is a present-tense verb, and the oath may be an answer to an oath, as He said: ﴿And they will surely swear, "We intended nothing but good"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 107]. The lam in ﴿wa la yahlifunna﴾ [al-Tawbah: 107] is the answer to an oath, and it is an oath. But since their swearing was not present but future, the nun was required, since it makes the imperfect unambiguously future.

The majority read ﴿bi-mawaqi'i﴾ in the plural. 'Umar, 'Abd Allah, Ibn 'Abbas, the people of Madinah, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read [p-214] bi-mawqi'i in the singular, intending the plural. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, Mujahid and others said: they are the stars of the Qur'an, which were sent down upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. This view is supported by His saying ﴿Indeed, it is a Qur'an﴾, since the pronoun refers to what is understood from His saying ﴿the positions of the stars﴾, meaning the stars of the Qur'an. It was also said: the stars are the planets and their positions. Mujahid and Abu 'Ubaydah said: at their rising and setting. Qatadah said: their positions are their places in the sky. Al-Hasan said: their positions are at the time of their falling on the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: at their dispersal after being shot as meteors. Whoever interpreted "the stars" as the planets makes the pronoun in "innahu" explained by the context of the speech, like His saying ﴿until it was hidden by the veil﴾ [Sad: 32].

In His swearing by the positions of the stars there is a secret in the glorifying of that which we do not know, and He magnified it greatly, saying: ﴿And indeed it is an oath, if you only knew, a great one﴾. The sentence sworn to is His saying ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾, and the oath is separated from its answer. The apparent view is that it is a parenthetical insertion between them, and in it there is a parenthetical insertion between the attribute and the qualified noun by His saying "if you only knew." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: ﴿And indeed it is an oath﴾ is an emphasis on the matter and an alerting from the one sworn by, and this is not a parenthesis between the two statements. Rather, this is a meaning intended for its gravity, and the parenthesis is only His saying "if you only knew." End of quotation. Karim (noble) is a description of praise that negates from it what is not fitting for it. Al-Zamakhshari said: "karim" means good and pleasing in its kind among books, or beneficial and of abundant benefits, or noble before Allah the Exalted.

﴿In a Book well-guarded﴾: that is, protected. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: it is the Book that is in the heaven. 'Ikrimah said: the Torah and the Gospel, as if He said: its nobility and honour were mentioned in a well-guarded Book, so the meaning according to this is citing the revealed books. It was also said: ﴿in a well-guarded Book﴾ means in the codices of the Muslims, protected from alteration and change, and at that time there were no codices, so this is a report of the unseen.

The apparent view is that His saying ﴿which none touches except the purified﴾ is a description of the noble Qur'an, so the purified are the angels. It was also said that ﴿which none touches﴾ is a description of the well-guarded Book. If the Book is the one in heaven, then the purified are also the angels, meaning none other than them can access it. Likewise according to the view of 'Ikrimah, they are the angels. If by the Book well-guarded is meant the written pages, then the meaning is that it should not be touched except by one who is in a state of purity among people. If the purified are the angels, then "none touches" is a negation, and the negated is supported by the reading of 'Abd Allah, "what touches it." If by them is meant those who are purified from disbelief and major impurity, then it may be a pure negation, and its ruling is that none touches it except the purified, even though one who is not purified may touch it, as in the hadith: "Its trees are not to be cut," meaning this is the ruling, even though cutting does occur. It may also be a negation intended as a prohibition, so the damma on the sin is an inflection. It may also be a prohibition, in which case, if the jussive were made explicit, it would appear, but since it was assimilated, it is jussive in estimation, and the damma on it is for the sake of the damma of the ha', as in the hadith: "Indeed we did not return it to you," where it is jussive and is jussive, and Sibawayh did not record in such cases of the assimilated jussive connected to the ha' of a masculine pronoun anything except the damma. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the view that "none touches" is a prohibition is a weak view, because if it is a statement, it stands in the position of an attribute, and His saying after that, "a revelation," is an attribute. If we make it a prohibition, its meaning becomes foreign, inserted between the attributes, and that is not good in describing speech, so consider it carefully. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud is "ma yamassuhu," and this strengthens what I preferred, that the statement whose meaning is that its worth and rank require that none touch it except one who is pure. End of quotation.

Abu Hayyan's commentary on Surah al-Waqi'ah (56:75–96), part 2 of 2

It is not necessary that *tanzīlun* (a sending down) be a qualifier (ṣifa, adjective). It may instead be the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada', the topic), in which case *lā yamassuhu* (﴿none touch it﴾) can be read as a prohibition (nahy). Here the scholars mention the ruling on touching the mushaf (the written copy of the Qur'an), which is discussed in jurisprudence (fiqh). There is nothing in the verse that proves a prohibition of this.

The majority read *al-mutahharūn* (﴿the purified﴾) as a passive participle (ism maf'ul) from *tahhara* in the intensive form. ʿĪsā read it likewise but in the form *aṭhara* (without doubling). It is also narrated from Nāfiʿ and Abū ʿAmr. Salmān al-Fārisī read *al-muṭahharūn* with a light ṭāʾ, a doubled hāʾ, and a kasra, as an active participle (ism fāʿil) from *taharra*, meaning "those who purify themselves." It is also narrated from him *al-muṭṭahharūn* with both letters doubled. Its original form is *al-mutaṭahharūn*, and the tāʾ was assimilated into the ṭāʾ (idgham, assimilation of consonants). This is narrated from al-Ḥasan and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAwf. It was also read *al-mutaṭahharūn*. It was read *tanzīlan* with a fatḥa, meaning "it was sent down, a sending down."

In ﴿Then is it of this discourse﴾, the pointer refers to the Qur'an. *Antum* (you) is addressed to the disbelievers. *Mudhinūn* (﴿disputing/being lax﴾): Ibn ʿAbbās said: "slackening in what is not lawful." He also said: "denying."

﴿And you make your provision﴾: that is, instead of thanking Allah for what He has provided you, by sending down the Qur'an upon you, you respond with denial. In other words, you put denial in the place of thanks. From this meaning is the verse of the rajaz poet:

*In place of the thanks of the people for favours,*
*is the branding of healthy camels and the gouging of eyes.*

ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās read *wa-tajʿalūna shukrakum* (and you make your thanks), and this is by way of explanation, since it differs from the written text (the rasm). Al-Haytham ibn ʿAdī related that in the dialect of the Azd Shanūʾa, *mā razaqa fulānun fulānan* means "what so-and-so thanked so-and-so for." It was said: the verse was revealed concerning the star-risings (anwāʾ) and attributing the watering (of the rain) to them, while *al-rizq* means the rain. The meaning is: what Allah provides you from the unseen. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: the commentators agreed that the verse is a rebuke to those who speak of rain, saying "this is by the star-rising of such and such," "this is by the star-rising of the Lion," "this is by the star-rising of Orion," and other such things.

The majority read *tukadhdhibūn* (you deny) from *takdhīb* (denial). ʿAlī and al-Mufaḍḍal from ʿĀṣim read it from *kadhib* (lying). The meaning of the first (denial) is that it is not from Allah, that is, the Qur'an or the rain, since they attribute that to the stars. The meaning of the second (lying) is their saying: the Qur'an is sorcery and fabrication, and the rain comes from the star-risings.

﴿Then why, when it reaches the throat, and you are at that moment looking on…﴾. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the arrangement of the verse is: "then why do you not send it back when it reaches the throat, if you are not held to account?" The second *falawlā* is repeated for emphasis, and the pronoun in *tarji'ūnahā* (you return it) refers to the soul (nafs). Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it is a halt at a point of deficiency, which requires considering that Allah is the owner of everything. *Antum* (you) is a reference to all of humankind. *Ḥīna'idhin* (at that time): at the time when it reaches the throat. *Tanẓurūn* (you look on): that is, at the one who is dying. ʿĪsā read *ḥīna'idhin* with a kasra on the nūn, following the vowel of the hamza in *idh*.

﴿And We are nearer to him than you, by knowledge and power﴾, ﴿but you do not see﴾: from the insight of the heart. Or (*aqrab*, nearer) means: Our angels and Our messengers. ﴿But you do not see﴾: from the sight of the eye.

Then the halt and the consideration return a second time with the wording of restriction. *Al-Madīn* means "one who is owned." Al-Akhṭal said:

*She raised me, and my upbringing was in her lap, the son of a slave-woman.*

It was said: "the son of a slave-girl," describing a slave, the son of a female slave. The end of the verse is:

*You see him upon a mule, going about.*

The meaning is: why do you not send back the soul that has reached the throat, if you are not owned and not subdued?

﴿If you are truthful﴾ in your nullifying and disbelief in the One who gives life and causes death, who originates and restores. This is because they held that the Qur'an is sorcery and fabrication, and that the rain that falls is by such and such a star-rising. That is a nullifying of the Creator and a rendering Him powerless.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: His saying *tarji'ūnahā* (you return it) stands in the place of its answer (the apodosis), and the explanations required by the restrictions (of the conditions), and *idhā* in His saying *falawlā idhā* (then why, when), and the repeated *in* (if). Some speech carries other speech, by way of brevity and economy. End of quotation. I say: *idhā* is not conditional. It does not stand in the place of its answer, rather it is an adverbial, non-conditional circumstantial phrase governed by the omitted *tarji'ūnahā* after *falawlā*, because *tarji'ūnahā* in the second restriction indicates it. So the first restriction came restricted to the time of reaching the throat, and the second restriction came conditional upon the negation of their being owned, and they cannot return it, since their being owned is existent. Thus they are subdued, with no power.

﴿But if he is of those brought near﴾, that is, the one who has died, ﴿those brought near﴾: they are the foremost.

The majority read *fa-rawḥun* (then rest) with a fatḥa on the rāʾ. ʿĀʾisha, from the Prophet (ﷺ), Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, Nūḥ al-Qāriʾ, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Ashhab, Shuʿayb ibn al-Ḥabḥāb, Sulaymān al-Taymī, al-Rabīʿ ibn Khaytham, Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī, Abū ʿImrān al-Jawnī, al-Kalbī, Fayyāḍ, ʿUbayd, ʿAbd al-Wārith from Abū ʿAmr, Yaʿqūb ibn Ṣayyān, Zayd, and Ruways from him read it with a ḍamma.

al-Ḥasan said: *al-rawḥ* means mercy, because it is like life for the one who is shown mercy. He also said: his spirit departs in a sweet basil (rayḥān). It was said: *al-rawḥ* means remaining (baqāʾ), that is, both of these are for him together: eternity with provision.

Mujāhid said: *al-rayḥān* means provision. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: rest. Abū al-ʿĀliya, Qatāda, and al-Ḥasan also said: *al-rayḥān* is this well-known plant of the world, and the one brought near receives a sweet basil from Paradise. al-Khalīl said: it is the container of every good herb in which the first buds of blossom appear.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said about al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn, may Allah be pleased with them both: "They are my two sweet basils of this world."
