﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ ﴿And indeed it is an oath, if you only knew, a great one﴾ ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾ ﴿in a Book well-guarded﴾ ﴿which none touches except the purified﴾ ﴿a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ ﴿Is it this discourse that you are scornful of?﴾ ﴿And you make your provision that you deny?﴾ ﴿Why, then, when it reaches the throat﴾ ﴿and you at that time are looking on﴾ ﴿and We are nearer to him than you, but you do not see﴾ ﴿Why, then, if you are not to be recompensed﴾ ﴿would you not bring it back, if you are truthful?﴾ ﴿As for if he is of those brought near﴾ ﴿then rest and provision and a Garden of bliss﴾ ﴿And as for if he is of the companions of the right﴾ ﴿then peace be upon you from the companions of the right﴾ ﴿And as for if he is of the deniers, the astray﴾ ﴿then a welcome of boiling water﴾ ﴿and roasting in Hellfire﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is the certain truth﴾ ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 75–96].

[p-212] The majority read ﴿fa-la uqsimu﴾. It was said that la is an extra, emphasizing particle, like its use in His saying ﴿so that the People of the Book may know﴾ [al-Hadid: 29], and the meaning is: "so I swear." It was also said that the negation is omitted, meaning: there is no truth to what the disbelievers say. Then he began with "uqsimu" ("I swear"). This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and some grammarians, but it is not permissible, because that would involve omitting the subject and predicate of la, and it is not an answer to a questioner who asked, so that it could be allowed, like the saying "la" in response to one who asks: "Is there anyone in the house?" It was also said that it is an emphatic particle of intensification, similar to an opening phrase of speech, resembling it in the oath except that it is common in speech and in other than oaths, and from it is the line:

*So no, by the father of its enemies, I will not betray it.*

My preferred view is that it is a lam whose fatha was prolonged, from which an alif was produced, like His saying:

*I seek refuge in Allah from the scorpion.*

Although this is rare, its counterpart appears in His saying ﴿so make hearts incline toward them from among the people﴾ [Ibrahim: 37], with a ya' after the hamza, which is in the reading of Hisham. So the meaning is: "then I swear," as in the reading of al-Hasan and 'Isa. Abu al-Fath explained al-Hasan's reading as based on an omitted subject, meaning "then indeed I swear," and al-Zamakhshari followed him in this. They went this way because it is a present-tense verb, and there is disagreement about swearing upon it. What Ibn 'Usfur and others chose is that a present-tense verb cannot be the object of an oath, so they had to treat the imperfect as the predicate of an omitted subject, making the sentence a nominal sentence, and then swearing upon it. Some grammarians held that swearing upon a present-tense verb is permissible, and this is what I choose. So you say: "By Allah, Zayd will indeed go out," and the poet's saying supports this:

*My Lord knows that my house is spacious.*

Al-Zamakhshari said, regarding al-Hasan's reading: the lam cannot be the lam of oath, for two reasons. One is that it should be accompanied by the emphatic nun, and omitting it is weak and ugly. The second is that la af'alanna in the answer of the oath is for the future, while the verb of the oath must be for the present. End of quotation. As for the first reason, there is disagreement about it: what he said is the view of the Basrans, while the Kufans prefer that, but they allow the two to alternate, so they permit "la adribanna Zaydan" and "adribanna 'Amran." As for the second reason, it is correct, but it is the one that we find preferable, that the lam in "la uqsimu" is the lam of oath, and "uqsimu" is a present-tense verb, and the oath may be an answer to an oath, as He said: ﴿And they will surely swear, "We intended nothing but good"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 107]. The lam in ﴿wa la yahlifunna﴾ [al-Tawbah: 107] is the answer to an oath, and it is an oath. But since their swearing was not present but future, the nun was required, since it makes the imperfect unambiguously future.

The majority read ﴿bi-mawaqi'i﴾ in the plural. 'Umar, 'Abd Allah, Ibn 'Abbas, the people of Madinah, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read [p-214] bi-mawqi'i in the singular, intending the plural. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, Mujahid and others said: they are the stars of the Qur'an, which were sent down upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. This view is supported by His saying ﴿Indeed, it is a Qur'an﴾, since the pronoun refers to what is understood from His saying ﴿the positions of the stars﴾, meaning the stars of the Qur'an. It was also said: the stars are the planets and their positions. Mujahid and Abu 'Ubaydah said: at their rising and setting. Qatadah said: their positions are their places in the sky. Al-Hasan said: their positions are at the time of their falling on the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: at their dispersal after being shot as meteors. Whoever interpreted "the stars" as the planets makes the pronoun in "innahu" explained by the context of the speech, like His saying ﴿until it was hidden by the veil﴾ [Sad: 32].

In His swearing by the positions of the stars there is a secret in the glorifying of that which we do not know, and He magnified it greatly, saying: ﴿And indeed it is an oath, if you only knew, a great one﴾. The sentence sworn to is His saying ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾, and the oath is separated from its answer. The apparent view is that it is a parenthetical insertion between them, and in it there is a parenthetical insertion between the attribute and the qualified noun by His saying "if you only knew." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: ﴿And indeed it is an oath﴾ is an emphasis on the matter and an alerting from the one sworn by, and this is not a parenthesis between the two statements. Rather, this is a meaning intended for its gravity, and the parenthesis is only His saying "if you only knew." End of quotation. Karim (noble) is a description of praise that negates from it what is not fitting for it. Al-Zamakhshari said: "karim" means good and pleasing in its kind among books, or beneficial and of abundant benefits, or noble before Allah the Exalted.

﴿In a Book well-guarded﴾: that is, protected. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: it is the Book that is in the heaven. 'Ikrimah said: the Torah and the Gospel, as if He said: its nobility and honour were mentioned in a well-guarded Book, so the meaning according to this is citing the revealed books. It was also said: ﴿in a well-guarded Book﴾ means in the codices of the Muslims, protected from alteration and change, and at that time there were no codices, so this is a report of the unseen.

The apparent view is that His saying ﴿which none touches except the purified﴾ is a description of the noble Qur'an, so the purified are the angels. It was also said that ﴿which none touches﴾ is a description of the well-guarded Book. If the Book is the one in heaven, then the purified are also the angels, meaning none other than them can access it. Likewise according to the view of 'Ikrimah, they are the angels. If by the Book well-guarded is meant the written pages, then the meaning is that it should not be touched except by one who is in a state of purity among people. If the purified are the angels, then "none touches" is a negation, and the negated is supported by the reading of 'Abd Allah, "what touches it." If by them is meant those who are purified from disbelief and major impurity, then it may be a pure negation, and its ruling is that none touches it except the purified, even though one who is not purified may touch it, as in the hadith: "Its trees are not to be cut," meaning this is the ruling, even though cutting does occur. It may also be a negation intended as a prohibition, so the damma on the sin is an inflection. It may also be a prohibition, in which case, if the jussive were made explicit, it would appear, but since it was assimilated, it is jussive in estimation, and the damma on it is for the sake of the damma of the ha', as in the hadith: "Indeed we did not return it to you," where it is jussive and is jussive, and Sibawayh did not record in such cases of the assimilated jussive connected to the ha' of a masculine pronoun anything except the damma. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the view that "none touches" is a prohibition is a weak view, because if it is a statement, it stands in the position of an attribute, and His saying after that, "a revelation," is an attribute. If we make it a prohibition, its meaning becomes foreign, inserted between the attributes, and that is not good in describing speech, so consider it carefully. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud is "ma yamassuhu," and this strengthens what I preferred, that the statement whose meaning is that its worth and rank require that none touch it except one who is pure. End of quotation.

Abu Hayyan's commentary on Surah al-Waqi'ah (56:75–96), part 2 of 2

It is not necessary that *tanzīlun* (a sending down) be a qualifier (ṣifa, adjective). It may instead be the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada', the topic), in which case *lā yamassuhu* (﴿none touch it﴾) can be read as a prohibition (nahy). Here the scholars mention the ruling on touching the mushaf (the written copy of the Qur'an), which is discussed in jurisprudence (fiqh). There is nothing in the verse that proves a prohibition of this.

The majority read *al-mutahharūn* (﴿the purified﴾) as a passive participle (ism maf'ul) from *tahhara* in the intensive form. ʿĪsā read it likewise but in the form *aṭhara* (without doubling). It is also narrated from Nāfiʿ and Abū ʿAmr. Salmān al-Fārisī read *al-muṭahharūn* with a light ṭāʾ, a doubled hāʾ, and a kasra, as an active participle (ism fāʿil) from *taharra*, meaning "those who purify themselves." It is also narrated from him *al-muṭṭahharūn* with both letters doubled. Its original form is *al-mutaṭahharūn*, and the tāʾ was assimilated into the ṭāʾ (idgham, assimilation of consonants). This is narrated from al-Ḥasan and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAwf. It was also read *al-mutaṭahharūn*. It was read *tanzīlan* with a fatḥa, meaning "it was sent down, a sending down."

In ﴿Then is it of this discourse﴾, the pointer refers to the Qur'an. *Antum* (you) is addressed to the disbelievers. *Mudhinūn* (﴿disputing/being lax﴾): Ibn ʿAbbās said: "slackening in what is not lawful." He also said: "denying."

﴿And you make your provision﴾: that is, instead of thanking Allah for what He has provided you, by sending down the Qur'an upon you, you respond with denial. In other words, you put denial in the place of thanks. From this meaning is the verse of the rajaz poet:

*In place of the thanks of the people for favours,*
*is the branding of healthy camels and the gouging of eyes.*

ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās read *wa-tajʿalūna shukrakum* (and you make your thanks), and this is by way of explanation, since it differs from the written text (the rasm). Al-Haytham ibn ʿAdī related that in the dialect of the Azd Shanūʾa, *mā razaqa fulānun fulānan* means "what so-and-so thanked so-and-so for." It was said: the verse was revealed concerning the star-risings (anwāʾ) and attributing the watering (of the rain) to them, while *al-rizq* means the rain. The meaning is: what Allah provides you from the unseen. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: the commentators agreed that the verse is a rebuke to those who speak of rain, saying "this is by the star-rising of such and such," "this is by the star-rising of the Lion," "this is by the star-rising of Orion," and other such things.

The majority read *tukadhdhibūn* (you deny) from *takdhīb* (denial). ʿAlī and al-Mufaḍḍal from ʿĀṣim read it from *kadhib* (lying). The meaning of the first (denial) is that it is not from Allah, that is, the Qur'an or the rain, since they attribute that to the stars. The meaning of the second (lying) is their saying: the Qur'an is sorcery and fabrication, and the rain comes from the star-risings.

﴿Then why, when it reaches the throat, and you are at that moment looking on…﴾. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the arrangement of the verse is: "then why do you not send it back when it reaches the throat, if you are not held to account?" The second *falawlā* is repeated for emphasis, and the pronoun in *tarji'ūnahā* (you return it) refers to the soul (nafs). Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it is a halt at a point of deficiency, which requires considering that Allah is the owner of everything. *Antum* (you) is a reference to all of humankind. *Ḥīna'idhin* (at that time): at the time when it reaches the throat. *Tanẓurūn* (you look on): that is, at the one who is dying. ʿĪsā read *ḥīna'idhin* with a kasra on the nūn, following the vowel of the hamza in *idh*.

﴿And We are nearer to him than you, by knowledge and power﴾, ﴿but you do not see﴾: from the insight of the heart. Or (*aqrab*, nearer) means: Our angels and Our messengers. ﴿But you do not see﴾: from the sight of the eye.

Then the halt and the consideration return a second time with the wording of restriction. *Al-Madīn* means "one who is owned." Al-Akhṭal said:

*She raised me, and my upbringing was in her lap, the son of a slave-woman.*

It was said: "the son of a slave-girl," describing a slave, the son of a female slave. The end of the verse is:

*You see him upon a mule, going about.*

The meaning is: why do you not send back the soul that has reached the throat, if you are not owned and not subdued?

﴿If you are truthful﴾ in your nullifying and disbelief in the One who gives life and causes death, who originates and restores. This is because they held that the Qur'an is sorcery and fabrication, and that the rain that falls is by such and such a star-rising. That is a nullifying of the Creator and a rendering Him powerless.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: His saying *tarji'ūnahā* (you return it) stands in the place of its answer (the apodosis), and the explanations required by the restrictions (of the conditions), and *idhā* in His saying *falawlā idhā* (then why, when), and the repeated *in* (if). Some speech carries other speech, by way of brevity and economy. End of quotation. I say: *idhā* is not conditional. It does not stand in the place of its answer, rather it is an adverbial, non-conditional circumstantial phrase governed by the omitted *tarji'ūnahā* after *falawlā*, because *tarji'ūnahā* in the second restriction indicates it. So the first restriction came restricted to the time of reaching the throat, and the second restriction came conditional upon the negation of their being owned, and they cannot return it, since their being owned is existent. Thus they are subdued, with no power.

﴿But if he is of those brought near﴾, that is, the one who has died, ﴿those brought near﴾: they are the foremost.

The majority read *fa-rawḥun* (then rest) with a fatḥa on the rāʾ. ʿĀʾisha, from the Prophet (ﷺ), Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, Nūḥ al-Qāriʾ, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Ashhab, Shuʿayb ibn al-Ḥabḥāb, Sulaymān al-Taymī, al-Rabīʿ ibn Khaytham, Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī, Abū ʿImrān al-Jawnī, al-Kalbī, Fayyāḍ, ʿUbayd, ʿAbd al-Wārith from Abū ʿAmr, Yaʿqūb ibn Ṣayyān, Zayd, and Ruways from him read it with a ḍamma.

al-Ḥasan said: *al-rawḥ* means mercy, because it is like life for the one who is shown mercy. He also said: his spirit departs in a sweet basil (rayḥān). It was said: *al-rawḥ* means remaining (baqāʾ), that is, both of these are for him together: eternity with provision.

Mujāhid said: *al-rayḥān* means provision. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: rest. Abū al-ʿĀliya, Qatāda, and al-Ḥasan also said: *al-rayḥān* is this well-known plant of the world, and the one brought near receives a sweet basil from Paradise. al-Khalīl said: it is the container of every good herb in which the first buds of blossom appear.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said about al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn, may Allah be pleased with them both: "They are my two sweet basils of this world."

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: *al-rayḥān* is that with which souls are delighted. ﴿Then rest﴾: then peace. *Fa-nuzulun*: the fā' is the answer to *ammā*, which came before it. *Ammā* is in the sense of a condition: "if he is of those brought near," "if he is of the companions of the right," "if he is of the denying, the astray," are conditions. When two conditions come together, the answer belongs to the first of them. The answer to the second is omitted, and for this reason the verb of the condition is in the past form, or accompanied by *lam*. The answer of *ammā* has taken its place. This is the position of Sībawayh. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī held that the fā' is the answer of *in*, and the answer of *ammā* is omitted, and he has a view agreeing with Sībawayh's position. al-Akhfash held that the fā' is the answer of *ammā* and the condition together. We have refuted these two positions in our book called *al-Tadhyīl wa-al-Takmīl fī Sharḥ al-Tashīl*.

The address in this is to the Messenger (ﷺ), meaning: you do not see among them, O Muhammad, except safety from punishment. Then for every one who takes heed from his community (ﷺ) there is a statement addressed to him: ﴿of the companions of the right﴾.

al-Ṭabarī said: the meaning is: peace to you, you who are of the companions of the right. Others said: the meaning is: it will be said to them, "Safe for you, because you are of the companions of the right." It was said: peace to you, O companion of the right, from your brothers, the companions of the right, that is, they greet you, like His saying: ﴿except the saying "Peace, peace"﴾ [al-Wāqiʿa 26].

The denying, astray ones are the companions of the left (*al-mash'ama*), the companions of the left hand.

The majority read *wa-taṣliyatun* (and burning) in the nominative, in conjunction with *fa-nuzulun*. Aḥmad ibn Mūsā, al-Minqarī, and al-Luʾluʾī from Abū ʿAmr read it in the genitive, in conjunction with *min ḥamīm* (of boiling water).

When the account of their conditions and where each category of them ends up has concluded, He confirmed that with His saying: ﴿Indeed, this﴾, that is, indeed this report mentioned in this surah ﴿is the truth of certainty﴾. It was said: this is from the construction of two synonyms for the sake of emphasis, as you say: "this is the certainty of certainty" and "the correctness of correctness," meaning that it is the ultimate in that, so the two have one meaning, and it is joined for emphasis. It was said: this is from the construction of a described thing with its description, making "the truth" distinct from "the certainty," that is, the established, the certainly known.

When the three categories had been mentioned at length, He, Exalted is He, commanded him to declare Him free from what does not befit Him of attributes. When He repeated the division briefly, He likewise commanded him to declare Him free and to glorify Him, to devote himself to worshipping his Lord, and to turn away from the sayings of the disbelievers who deny the Resurrection, the Reckoning, and the Recompense.

It appears that *sabbiḥ* (glorify) is transitive sometimes by itself, as in His saying: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Aʿlā 1], and *yusabbiḥūhu*; and sometimes by a preposition, as in His saying: ﴿So glorify with the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾. The word *al-ʿaẓīm* (the Mighty) may be a qualifier of *ism* (name), and it may be a qualifier of *rabbika* (your Lord).
